items.title: Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
paragraphs: Andy Burnham has ruled out an early general election in the next 12 months, after opposition parties suggested one would be called.
The next UK general election must be held by August 2029, and there has been speculation that the prime minister is preparing for an earlier poll.

Asked directly if he would call a snap election within the next year, the prime minister told broadcasters: "I don't know how many times I've done this now but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months."
He said he was focusing on people over the Labour Party, adding: "I'm not thinking about myself. I'm not thinking about my own party and its prospects."
Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch suggested Burnham may go to the country early.

She said the Conservative Party was "coming back" after it slumped in popularity at the end of 14 years in government, telling BBC South East: "This is an era of political volatility and multi-party politics."
She added: "I do think Andy Burnham is going to call an election sooner than he is saying... all the policies he announced are for after an election."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said in September he believed there would be an election "next spring".
"I believe there must be a general election because Andy Burnham has no mandate - the messiah without a mandate, we deserve a general election on who continues to govern this country."

Burnham was elected MP in June after the Makerfield by-election, before securing the Labour Party leadership and becoming prime minister after Sir Keir Starmer lost the support of Labour MPs and quit Downing Street.
He has since outlined a number of ambitions, which has led some to question whether he will try to secure a fresh mandate before 2029.
One of these issues is Brexit, where Burnham has said he wants an "honest conversation" about the UK's future relationship with the EU.
On Wednesday, he promised to stick to the red lines in his party's 2024 manifesto on EU freedom of movement, the single market and customs union "for the whole of this Parliament".
The current Parliamentary term runs until the next general election.

Burnham has repeatedly denied he is seeking a snap poll. He told broadcasters on Wednesday: "We've got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage."

items.title: Microsoft is ending Copilot support on smart TVs
paragraphs: A notification on LG TVs reveals that Copilot functionality is soon going away on all TVs.
A notification on LG TVs reveals that Copilot functionality is soon going away on all TVs.
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Nearly two years after LG and Samsung announced at CES 2025 that their latest smart TVs would include access to Microsoft’s Copilot, the company is ending support for the AI assistant’s functionality on all TVs this year, according to a report by Windows Central.

The news comes not from an official announcement from LG, Samsung, or Microsoft, but from an on-screen notification that appeared on Windows Central’s Zac Bowden’s webOS-powered LG TV earlier today. “Microsoft has recently decided to end support for Copilot functionality on all TVs, including the Copilot-enabled feature available on our LG TVs. As a result, the Copilot-enabled feature on your TV is no longer available and may stop functioning shortly,” the notification explains. It doesn’t specify exactly when Copilot will stop working on smart TVs, but says the feature is “scheduled for discontinuation during 2026” and a specific date is “subject to Microsoft’s timeline.”

Last December, LG faced backlash after an update to webOS added an unremovable Microsoft Copilot shortcut to their TVs that opened the AI assistant’s web app in a browser. LG eventually decided to allow the shortcut to be deleted following many users expressing their frustration online with it being added without their approval.

Microsoft Copilot primarily served as a friendly AI-powered companion on Samsung and LG smart TVs that users could chat with, ask questions about what was currently on screen, or get recommendations for TV shows and movies. But earlier this year, Microsoft introduced a new Copilot “super app” that bundled multiple AI capabilities including chat, agents, and coding into a single interface as part of a push towards positioning Copilot more as a business and productivity tool, and less as a digital companion.

items.title: Babydoll singer says life will 'never be the same again' after UK number one
paragraphs: Jamie Miller says "nothing feels normal" anymore but he is trying to "live in the moment" as he comes to terms with his history-making song Babydoll.
Last week the 29-year-old became the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years with the viral TikTok hit.

The singer, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, said his dreams had "come true" and life would "never be the same again" after a challenging few years in which he even had to give up on music for a time.
Miller said the last year had been "insane" as he has gone from watching Gavin and Stacey with his parents to getting messages on his social media from the cast.
Miller made history when he became the first Welsh artist to top the singles chart since Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder.
He is also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 timeless festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone.
"It just doesn't feel real. To actually live my dreams the way that it's coming about right now," he said.

The song found fame on TikTok when actress Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos featuring the track. But Miller said the "genuineness" of the track also made it stand out as his first song since his hiatus.
"I went through a really, really hard few years in my personal life, and I took two years off music," he said.
"There's a genuineness to how I sound in the song. The world's in a little bit of a dark place right now so maybe that's why it's made people come together."

items.title: Surprise: The Google Xreal glasses debut at a Meta-beating $1,099
paragraphs: In this economy, how often does a product get less expensive before its debut? That just happened with the Google / Xreal Aura, the lightweight 95-gram glasses with a tethered Android XR compute puck and multiple virtual screens that just went on sale today. Xreal and Google have just announced the headset costs $1,099 through the end of the year, down from the $1,279 that Xreal was charging for early preorders last month.

I expect that’s because at $1,279, they were going head to head with Meta’s VR Glasses, and that’s tough competition for Google and Xreal’s new product. The Xreal Aura has one of the widest fields of view for transparent glasses yet at 70 degrees diagonal, but that’s still not huge and transparent glasses have other tradeoffs.

Perhaps just as importantly, you no longer have to navigate a maze of reservations, preorders, and Founder’s Editions if you want to buy the new Google glasses (so long as you live in a launch country). You can just order the 12GB RAM + 256GB storage model for $1,099 in the US, Canada, and South Korea, or the 16GB + 512GB for a discounted $1,299, with “units expected to begin shipping in mid-November.” It’ll go on sale November 2nd in Japan, with broader availability next year.
And if you did preorder at the original price, Xreal GM and spokesperson Ralph Jodice tells The Verge that the company will automatically and instantly refund you the difference.

Xreal and Google say that the headset will launch with over 150 “made-for-XR experiences,” some of which you can see in Google’s blog post and read about in Xreal’s press release, as well as new immersive films like Andy Serkis’s Nevatars and Galapagos: the Last Eden. You’ll be able to plug a computer or handheld game console right into the USB-C compute puck to mirror it to the glasses, alongside your virtual windows, and you can ask Google’s Gemini AI about what you’re seeing.

Google also writes that Google Photos is getting an XR update: “This year, Google Photos will include a new spatial gallery that wraps your library around you. You can pan from an entire year down to a single day with your hands, then open a favorite memory in 3D.”

Xreal is also partnering with GameSir to offer a wireless gamepad with a dedicated Gemini key (and a charging dock, and swappable D-pads) and is announcing a folding portable wireless keyboard; we don’t have price, release date, or other details for those.

items.title: Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
paragraphs: Income tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation.

John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end.
The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets.

But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.
Freezing thresholds is often dubbed a stealth tax because, unlike raising the headline rates, it is not as obvious on your payslip.
It has been a useful way for chancellors from Rishi Sunak onwards to raise more money to help pay for things like defence, the NHS, schools and support for the sick, disabled and the elderly.

The amount of extra money brought in by freezing tax thresholds has risen steadily every year, and is due to reach £58bn by 2030-31, more than the UK government spends on transport and not far off current defence spending.

They hit you hardest if your income is close to one of the tax thresholds, but anyone who gets a pay rise is affected, as long as you earn enough to pay tax. Only people earning under £12,570 - the personal allowance threshold - pay no income tax.
By 2031 an extra 6.8 million people will be paying tax who wouldn't have if the personal allowance had not been frozen, the OBR calculates.
The state pension is currently just below the personal allowance threshold, and pensioners looked set to be drawn into paying tax from next April, when the basic state pension rises to £13,036.

However, the chancellor is putting in place a new separate Pension Tax Allowance, which will ensure that low-income pensioners, with income up to the value of the full new state pension, will not pay income tax.
The personal allowance threshold is set for the whole UK, so people in Scotland will also be affected, although other tax bands there vary, external.
National Insurance Contributions (Nics) are levied according to the same thresholds.

Wages usually go up year-on-year to cover the rising cost of living. Normally tax thresholds would also be raised in line with rising prices. Currently that isn't happening - the thresholds have been "frozen" at 2021 levels.
So, as your pay rises, a bigger proportion of it ends up above the threshold where you start to pay tax.

If the personal allowance had risen with inflation over the last five years, you would now be able to take home the first £16,070 of your salary without paying any income tax. Instead you pay 20% on anything you earn above £12,570.
As incomes rise, frozen thresholds also mean more and more people are dragged into the higher, 40%, tax bracket.
An extra 5.4 million will be higher rate taxpayers by 2031, thanks to the freeze, according to the OBR.
If thresholds had risen with inflation you would have had to be earning £64,470 this year before you tipped into the higher tax bracket.
As it is, with thresholds frozen at 2021 levels, you pay the higher rate on anything you earn over £50,271.
If you were already earning more than the threshold and you get a pay rise, a bigger proportion of your earnings will be taxed at the higher rate.
Almost one in four taxpayers will pay some of their tax at the higher rate by 2031, according to the government's official forecaster.
The same principle - that rising income can push you into a new tax bracket - applies to the additional, 45%, rate that is charged on a person's income over £125,140.
Wages have risen sharply to keep up with inflation in recent years, making the impact of the first five years of this policy quite noticeable, and that is set to continue.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) says if Healey had unfrozen the personal allowance this week, instead of keeping it in place until 2031, basic rate taxpayers would have saved up to £198 in tax a year.
Higher rate taxpayers would save £395 a year.
However, for people in the middle of the earnings range, a cut to Nics introduced in 2024 has offset the higher income tax bill.
How much of a difference "unfreezing" thresholds will make in four years' time depends on how fast wages are going up at that point.

There is no fundamental principle at stake, no point that is the "right" level for tax thresholds. Before the financial crisis the personal allowance was much smaller than today, and it was allowed to grow until the pandemic hit. Even in 2031 you'll be able to take home a bigger proportion of your earnings before income tax than you could back in 2008.

items.title: ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of Spain’s second deadly train crash in 10 months
paragraphs: Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.
“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.
Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.

“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”

The Peruvian stood recounting the details of Wednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.

Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south of Spain. Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.

As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.

Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.
Fredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines who now live in Dubai, were on the Iryo train, and Fredrich was sent flying by the impact.

“One guy was shouting, ‘Get out! Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. We just got as far away from the train as we could.”
Eventually, buses arrived to ferry the lightly injured survivors to Urda – although the Barileas said they were too shocked and confused to know where exactly they had been brought.

“It all happened in a split second,” said Arabella. “The table we were sitting at just disappeared in the crash. I feel like we’re on our second life. You never know what could happen. We’re very grateful.”

Around the couple, people queued patiently on the street as they waited to board coaches. Wearing torn and bloodstained clothes and, in some cases, bandages on their heads, they stared, mute and uncomprehending. Spain may have been in mourning, as the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said during his visit to Urda, but many of those fortunate enough to survive Spain’s second fatal rail crash in less than a year were still too deep in shock to begin grieving.

Ata Yelkaya, a young tourist from Turkey, usually takes the bus when he travels around Spain. On Wednesday, however, he had decided to try the Iryo. Sleepy and assuming his train had come to a halt at a station, he had switched off his tablet and pulled up his hood in preparation for a nap. At 8.53am, he felt what he would later learn was the impact of the Renfe train smashing into the carriages behind him.

“I woke up with a bump and hit my head on the seat in front of me,” he said, “I looked across at an elderly couple near me and saw that the woman had a cut in her eyebrow. That’s when I knew something serious had happened.”
When he looked out of the window, he saw the carriages behind his – carriage No 5 – had come off the track and that many people had been killed or injured.

“Everyone was in shock but I tried to help other people get off the train,” he said. “I’m from Turkey and I lived through the 2023 earthquake there, so I stayed calm and tried to think about what to do and how to get out. It was only when I got out and saw some of the dead people that it hit me. I think everyone was in shock; too shocked even to panic or to scream.”

Wednesday’s disaster stirs memories of the Adamuz rail crash in January, in which 46 people died. Once again, a small town has found itself at the centre of a national disaster and, once again, local people have rallied to help, bringing food and water to a hall that had been set up as a centre for those searching for their relatives.

But, as also happened at Adamuz, the solidarity and kindness on display is likely to turn to anger over the coming hours as people seek answers as to how one of Europe’s most modern and extensive high-speed rail networks could experience two deadly accidents that have between them claimed at least 114 lives in the space of just 10 months. With a snap general election just a month away, many voters could use their votes to register their fury over another rail disaster. The “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash – as Spain’s transport minister has called them – will need to be explained as swiftly thoroughly as possible.

For all the rush to action and unity on display, there was also a sickening sense of deja vu. One woman from Urda, who had spent the morning driving people to town from the crash site, had few words to describe what she had seen and heard.
“Mejor no verlo,” she said – “it’s better not to see something like this”. Again.

items.title: Here’s where to preorder the latest MacBook Pros
paragraphs: Apple finally showed off its 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops that have the PROLED XDR display at the October 2026 “Pro and Tell” event. The long-awaited laptops feature a Tandem OLED display with full touch capabilities, while also cutting some weight, and bringing back the glowing Apple logo. While a little less exciting, there’s also an updated 14-inch MacBook Pro that includes Apple’s M6 CPU, along with improved wireless connectivity. Like the generation before it, this is a small, somewhat iterative update, without substantial new features beyond performance gains.

Alongside the MacBook updates, Apple also took the opportunity to update the iMac with M6 chips, which start at $1,499, with the same color variants as the previous generation. Lastly, the iPad Mini got some love, with a larger OLED display that has smaller bezels, as well as water resistance, plus a slimmer and lighter design.

Preorders for the 14-inch MacBook Pro are live at Apple and Best Buy, while the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is currently only available for preorder at Apple, although we expect Best Buy to follow suit soon. For anyone looking to get their hands on either system, we’ve compiled all the information on configuration options, pricing, and retailer availability below.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model, or $3,399 for the 16-inch version, and start shipping on Friday, November 6th. There are two CPU options, with each offering an optional upgrade to add more cores. The base 14-inch M5 Pro model starts with 24GB of memory and 1TB of storage, and the upgraded $4,499 14-inch model that has the M5 Max starts with 36GB of memory and 2TB of storage, with maximum memory and storage options depending on CPU choice. There are both space black and silver colors, and the option to upgrade to nano-texture glass for $150.

The biggest new feature here is the PROLED XDR display. In addition to finally adding touch capabilities to the macOS lineup, the screen features a Tandem OLED panel, which Apple says can reach an impressive 2,000 nits at peak brightness, with a 120Hz refresh rate. This update also marks the return of the glowing Apple logo on the back of the shell, a feature that disappeared as the systems slimmed down years ago.

The updated 14-inch MacBook Pro ships on Friday, November 6th, and comes in three CPU options. The M6 version with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage starts at $1,999, the model with the upgraded M5 Pro chip and 24GB of memory and 1TB of storage starts at $2,499, and the top-end model with the M5 Max chip with 36GB of memory and 2TB of storage starts at $4,099.

There are memory and storage upgrades available as well, with up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage on the M6 version, and 48GB of memory and 4TB of storage on the M5 Pro. The M5 Max has more limited options, but you can configure it with up to 128GB of memory and 8TB of storage if you also opt for the upgraded CPU. It’s available in both black and silver, with the option to upgrade to the nano-texture display for an extra $150.
Best Buy is currently offering to include a $100 gift card with the purchase of an M6-powered MacBook Pro. The card will automatically appear in your cart under the “Complete your purchase” section.

items.title: Sam Fender pre-sale moved after 'bot attack'
paragraphs: Sam Fender has rescheduled the pre-sale for his tour's homecoming show after a "sophisticated bot attack" reportedly affected a ticketing website.

In a post on Instagram, the 32-year-old said he had been told the site Gigantic had been hit for his shows at St James' Park in Newcastle in summer 2027, prompting him to move the sale back 24 hours to 09:30 GMT on Thursday.
It came days after he removed a ticket category from sale due to his unhappiness with the costs for fans, which he said were out of his control.
Gigantic said its system had detected an "unusually high volume of suspicious activity" resulting in error messages on its site and it had halted the pre-sale to protect fans.
Fender announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour last week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester.

The musician from North Shields did not give details for any other venues being affected by the "bot attack", but a source told the BBC they did not have any issues buying tickets for the London show.
Fender wrote: "Being told that there's been a sophisticated bot attack to the Gigantic ticket site which is impacting the St James' Park pre-sale.
"We're going to have to move the Newcastle pre-sale to 09:30 tomorrow to ensure real fans get the tickets."
Gigantic said in a statement: "We know how frustrating this morning was for many of you, and we're sorry.
"Fans should be able to buy tickets fairly, and that is what we're working to make sure happens."

items.title: New book revisits the 2023 killing of an unhoused man in crisis on the NYC subway
paragraphs: Jordan Neely was shouting threats on the NYC subway. Fellow passenger Daniel Penny put Neely into a chokehold and killed him. Journalist Anand Giridharadas believes both men felt abandoned. Above, protestors rally in support of Neely in New York City on May 24, 2023. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images hide caption

On May 1, 2023, an unhoused Black man named Jordan Neely boarded the New York City subway. For years, Neely had drawn crowds with his Michael Jackson impersonation, but on that day he was in crisis, shouting threats and frightening fellow passengers.

A white former Marine named Daniel Penny stepped in, putting Neely into a chokehold for six minutes, killing him. Later, a video of the encounter divided the country. To some, Penny was doing what the police weren't there to do. To others, Neely was a victim, another Black man whose life had been treated as disposable.

Journalist Anand Giridharadas spent more than two years investigating what the video couldn't show. He wanted to write a story "that would take us to the heart of America and what it means to live in this country, in this moment." When tragic stories become social media fodder, Giridharadas says, "human beings become caricatures."

In December 2024, Penny was acquitted of criminally negligent homicide after a jury hung on a second degree manslaughter charge and the prosecution dismissed it. Within days of the verdict, Vice President-elect JD Vance invited Penny to the Army-Navy game alongside President-elect Trump. Soon afterward, a Silicon Valley venture capital firm gave him a job.
In his new book, Man in the Mirror: Hope, Struggle, and Belonging in an American City, Giridharadas posits that both men felt let down by the systems that should have protected them.

"I think Jordan Neely had felt abandoned for a very long time, and had reason to feel that way," Giridharadas says. "Daniel Penny would claim that he felt abandoned in terms of law enforcement not being there, and in terms of all the systems that had allowed Jordan Neely to be in that subway car in that condition instead of all of the other conditions that he might have been in had there been a better system of care."

Giridharadas says it's that sense of abandonment that leads people to take matters into their own hands, often with tragic results: "I think it behooves us to think about the condition in which we've left people, this sense of abandonment that we've allowed to be so pervasive that decent people feel like maybe there's no other route for folks besides just DIYing it."
On Jordan Neely's criminal record and the city's attempt at rehabilitation

He had a record of interactions with the police that went back more than a decade. But it was very trivial stuff at the beginning. It was essentially the stuff of what it takes to be homeless in New York, jumping turnstiles, sleeping rough. And then in more recent years, it had gotten more serious and he'd committed a couple of violent crimes, assaults, punching a woman in the face, things like that. And he had gone to Rikers. He'd been charged. And then as part of this alternative to incarceration program — and there are programs like this popping up around the country, where folks get an alternative to going to prison that is considered more restorative, more in line with actually helping people who have substance issues or other issues — he gets to avail of one of these programs. Prosecution, defense, they all agree. And he gets sent to this kind of rehab facility in the Bronx instead of prison. And one day, he just walks out of that facility.

And then, in April 2023, just a few weeks before he died, he is [at] Coney Island, one of the terminal points on the subway system, and he's acting erratically on the platform. Outreach workers try to deal with him to no avail. The cops have some interaction with him, but they don't actually realize that it is the guy who is out with a warrant for his arrest because he walked out of this program. And the outreach workers who were there that night don't quite realize that he's a guy that their agency knows very well, just maybe not those individual workers. And he sort of runs off into the night. And a few weeks later, he's dead on the floor of a different subway car.
On Daniel Penny's origins in West Islip, Long Island

These towns in central Long Island have this very complicated relationship [with New York City]. … On the one hand, it's very out of the city, but it's right there. A lot of people commute in every day for work. Some don't. These are towns that were largely populated by white flight in the last several decades. … In many ways, these are towns that are almost like middle-class refugee camps from the squalor and terror of New York City.

Maybe even understanding immigrant stories is a more helpful framework for understanding these places. … Immigrants have very complicated relationships with the places they leave. We don't think about that with places that are 45 minutes away from a metropolis, but I actually think that is the way to understand the town in which Daniel Penny grew up. … These are communities where there's often a contempt, often barely concealed, for all the people one wanted to get away from, when one left.

I can't know what's in his heart. I didn't sense that kind of sadness or remorse. And not only did I not necessarily pick that up in that brief conversation we had at his victory party a year and a half after the incident, but one of the things that's striking in both the bodycam video on the scene when they first get there, as well as the interrogation ... is that even in those moments, forget remorse, he doesn't even seem to have curiosity about what may have happened to that guy.

He sort of gave the impression of a kind of blankness, ideologically. And that was one of the things that then became very strange, that all these people really wanted him to be their symbol and projected onto him all these ideas. And then he, of course, willingly embraced it. He embraced the money that came from it. And then, most dramatically still, at the end of the case, not only was he content to appear with JD Vance and Donald Trump at the Army-Navy game, but shortly thereafter, he got a job offer that gobsmacked many people. This is someone who, I think, has not graduated from college. He was offered a job as a partner at the venture capital firm in Silicon Valley called Andreessen Horowitz. ... He was made partner on their American dynamism team, which is a team that invests in startups that do weapons systems and drones and other things supposedly in the national interest.
On the politicization of the case and parallels with Luigi Mangione

I had spent the last year and a half hearing Daniel Penny's people make an argument that was basically like, "The system wasn't there, the system wasn't responsive. Daniel Penny stepped into a void and did what he had to do, took matters into his own hands because of this void." And then in the jury deliberations during that moment was the Mangione assassination of Brian Thompson, of United Health Care. And as that case started to become better known, a similar argument started to develop around Luigi Mangione, this time on the parts of the left instead of parts of right that Luigi Mangione was stepping into this void of a cruel healthcare system and stepping in because so many people were abandoned and he felt abandoned. …

And then Hawk Newsome, Black Lives Matter activist in New York, says, yes ... if they're gonna have vigilantes, we need Black vigilantes. But we also need to make our own schools, we need to have our own media, we have to have our own everything.

And I just thought to myself, gosh, is this the last kind of common thread? The idea that you could hear on the far right, the far left, and elsewhere that we're abandoned, the system's rigged, no one's listening, take matters into your own hands. The sense of, somebody step up. Somebody do something.
Anna Bauman and Thea Chaloner produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

items.title: Fed holds interest rates steady even as inflation remains stubborn
paragraphs: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and his colleagues voted to hold their benchmark interest rate steady Wednesday. The central bank had raised rates in September, in an effort to curb persistent inflation. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images North America hide caption
The Federal Reserve opted not to raise interest rates Wednesday, but signaled that it's not retreating from the fight against stubborn inflation.
The central bank renewed its pledge to deliver price stability, a goal that's been made more difficult by a spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran.
"Inflation remains elevated," the Fed's rate-setting committee acknowledged in a statement.

At its last policy meeting in September, the Fed raised rates for the first time in more than three years. Since then, data has shown inflation has continued to accelerate, with consumer prices in September up 3.7% from a year ago — a bigger annual increase than the previous month.
"It's 'wrong way," says Dan North, a senior economist at the insurance company Allianz Trade. "That inflation line is going up, not down."
The decision not to adjust interest rates comes less than a week before votes are tallied in the midterm election, which may have contributed to the Fed's caution.
"It would be suspicious if there were a hike before the midterm," North said.

After a pause at this week's meeting, Fed policymakers are widely expected to raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December, in an effort to tamp down demand and bring prices under control.

Two members of the rate-setting committee wanted to move more quickly. Fed governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack of the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank voted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point on Wednesday, while a majority of Fed policymakers opted to stand pat.
The Federal Reserve's benchmark rate — currently 3.75 to 4% — helps to establish the cost of other short-term lending for things like credit cards.

Longer-term interest rates are set by the bond market but can also be influenced by Fed decisions. Mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, before easing slightly. The high cost of home loans has been a drag on the housing market, which has been in a slump for the last four years.

Other parts of the economy are less sensitive to rising interest rates. The booming investment in artificial intelligence, for example, shows no sign of slowing down, no matter how much the Fed tries to tap on the brakes.
"The A.I. companies don't care what interest rate they have to pay," North says.
The frenzied push to build A.I. data centers is pushing up prices for construction materials and electronic equipment.
Consumer spending has also remained resilient, fueled in part by upper-income shoppers who benefit from the rising stock market.
That's not the case for less wealthy families, whose wages are not keeping pace with the rising cost of living. Average wages rose just 3% for the 12 months ending in September.

"Lower and middle-income Americans are having a real struggle," says Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. " Their purchasing power is actually declining. And that's a pretty uncomfortable place to be. And that likely goes to explain to a large degree why people don't feel very good about the economy."

items.title: You can see every red flag in Theranos 2.0
paragraphs: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

From afar, it’s easy to look back at the Theranos debacle and scream at Nathan Fielder that, obviously, Elizabeth Holmes is lying in You Can See Everything. In the weeks since the movie’s release, journalists and whistleblowers alike have rushed to remind moviegoers of Holmes’ numerous documented lies. Chief among the facts: The Theranos device never worked as advertised. But Fielder’s aim with this film wasn’t relitigating Theranos. Even the most mind-bending of three-hour documentaries doesn’t have enough time to fully tackle the quagmire that was the secretive biotech startup.

It’s worth remembering that Theranos was a prime example of overinflating what technology can do. It sure would be nice if a single droplet of blood could be run in a magical machine and beep boop — you’ve got accurate results for over a hundred diagnostic tests. It’s a compelling concept, but the existing science doesn’t support the idea. As I wrote in last week’s Optimizer, you simply can’t test for every disease from blood alone. Sometimes, a blood test is merely part of a multistep process to rule out what you don’t have. A finger prick carries a higher risk of rupturing blood cells, which can skew test results. Your finger is more prone to surface contamination because hands are dirty by nature. Compared to drawing blood from a vein, a finger prick may not be purely blood — it often mixes with interstitial fluid, diluting the sample. Different biomarkers can require wholly different testing procedures, making the small volume collected difficult to work with. These are just some of the practical challenges Theranos had to solve to be better than the clinical gold standard. It couldn’t, and that’s why they had to fake it by bringing in Siemens devices that used traditional blood testing methods.
That makes it even more astonishing that Holmes and her partner Billy Evans spend a chunk of the film actively working on what Evans casually calls Theranos 2.0.

This new venture, Haemanthus, involves a similar diagnostic device that uses… lasers. The official line is that Holmes is not helming the effort, but Evans refers to it as “getting the band back together.” The film purposefully blurs the lines between truth and lies. But with nascent health tech, it’s genuinely hard for the average person to distinguish promising medical advancements from snake oil.

If you left You Can See Everything wondering if there’s any truth to using lasers to diagnose conditions — you don’t have to watch microbiology videos at twice the speed to find out. Instead, here are a few extra tips when it comes to spotting shenanigans straight out of the wellness grifter playbook.
In the documentary, Fielder likens Holmes to a magician. Technology, no matter how powerful or well crafted, is never magic.

But going along with Fielder’s metaphor, magicians succeed through misdirection. Evans presents lasers in the film as though they’re a little-known marvel — a key technology Theranos was missing — and that Haemanthus will be the first to make them truly useful. Based on a patent published by The New York Times, Haemanthus uses Raman spectroscopy. For the record, Raman spectroscopy does involve lasers, but it’s not a new technology. It was first discovered in 1928.

In a nutshell, this laser tech is used to identify chemical structures in a molecule. There are myriad biological and medical uses for it, including noninvasively studying tissue samples. But will it, as a New York Times report describes, “identify and qualify biomarkers such as glucose and hormones” and then use AI to “detect cancer and infections”?

Researchers are exploring using this tech to diagnose early-stage cancers. They’re also looking into using it for glucose monitoring. Does that mean this is a better method than what currently exists? Maybe for certain cases, but probably not in every scenario. In medicine, it’s common to require multiple tests for diagnosis. Similarly, there are often multiple ways to treat the same condition. It’s often a game of weighing pros and cons for various approaches. There are too many unknown factors to accurately comment on Haemanthus, but it’s concerning that Evans zeroes in on lasers like they’re a panacea for everything that plagued Theranos.

When investors, journalists, and the public ask hard questions, founders love to sprinkle technology into their rhetoric like it’s fairy dust. You can see it happening right now with AI. But tech is a tool. Any tool will have pros and cons, situations it excels in and scenarios it’s ill suited for. It’s not always a grift, but anytime an executive shows signs of magical thinking or inflates what technology can do, your bullshit alarm should be ringing.

In recent history, I can think of exactly one time the public health sector truly hauled ass to make something happen: the covid-19 vaccine. The vaccine took roughly 10 months to develop, compared to the typical five-to-15-year timeline. But even then, it was a Herculean effort requiring global coordination and tens of billions of dollars, largely from the government. (That’s not including the billions invested in researching mRNA vaccines during the three decades prior to the pandemic.) It was a heartening feat of human ingenuity — but again, it took 10 months built on 30 years of foundational research and several billion dollars.

So it’s an immediate red flag when Evans says in the documentary that Haemanthus would have a novel, revolutionary prototype working in about a year. Case in point, he said that in 2023, and it’s already 2026. But even if lasers were the key to everything, there’s no way in hell something like this would breeze through the regulatory process.

Not much is known about Haemanthus. It has no website, unless you count a sparse LinkedIn page that says the company has two to 10 employees and is working on “AI-native sensors for health,” a technology that “captures thousands of biomarkers.” The bulk of what’s publicly known comes from You Can See Everything and a 2025 New York Times article, which states Haemanthus is building a device that uses a “laser to scan blood, saliva, or urine from pets and analyze the sample on a molecular level.” (The startup is apparently aiming to do veterinary tests first before perhaps eventually graduating to humans.) Its “long-term goal” is a “stamp-size, wearable version” of its product for humans, which will “require three years and $70 million.”

This is an incredibly expeditious timeline for any medical device, let alone a novel one. Not least because the biggest names in wearable technology right now can only detect — not diagnose — signs of perhaps two or three conditions. The holy grail is considered noninvasive continuous glucose monitoring, an endeavor that started in 1975 and that Apple has been rumored to be working on for over 15 years now. In 2023, I did a deep dive into why you shouldn’t expect this to arrive on smartwatches anytime soon. The reasons ranged from weak signals and regulatory mazes to skin color impacting how light reflects and battery life. In 2026, not much has changed on this front.

Meanwhile, take the continuous glucose monitor. Attempts to monitor glucose levels started in the mid-1800s, but a portable way to monitor glucose didn’t emerge until the 1960s. The first FDA-approved CGM was the Medtronic MiniMed in 1999, but it could only be worn for three days, and data couldn’t be viewed live. A clinician had to review it and inform the patient afterward. The first real-time CGM wasn’t available until 2004, the first over-the-counter CGMs didn’t hit the market until 2024, and only this year did Abbott announce a CGM that can measure two biomarkers.

AI advancements could theoretically help remove some technological roadblocks that may, in turn, speed up the overall process. But you know what AI doesn’t really replace? The absolutely labyrinthine regulatory approval and clearance process. You can have a product made and ready to go, only to have it held up in regulatory limbo for years. It’s happened to several Withings products. The infamous wearable taint zapper took six years, an untold number of testing bunnies, and at least a million dollars to hit the market. It’s why wearable companies are currently lobbying in Washington, likely spending mountains of cash to lower these hurdles.
So the next time a biotech startup promises something revolutionary relatively fast, it’s usually a pretty good sign they’re either delusional or not telling you the whole truth.

Another red flag with Theranos was that the company never published its research or submitted it for peer review. Haemanthus’ pseudo-secrecy — if you really wanted to build in stealth, why would you talk about it at length in a documentary? — is another concerning sign.

Perhaps because of Theranos, health tech companies have begun publishing more of their science. Oura, Apple, and Google are all great examples of companies that have published clinical and peer-reviewed research in reputable journals, as well as white papers explaining their features.

The act of publishing doesn’t get you a hall pass from scrutiny. Science-washing in the wellness and health sectors is rampant, with some companies using consumer perception studies as “evidence” instead of more rigorous studies. Or, if clinical studies are done, they’re often more of a vanity project than a groundbreaking revelation. Lastly, not all peer-reviewed papers are created equal. You have to be able to read and analyze the fine print to tell if the study itself was done well.

However, the absence of any reviewable research should sound the alarm for anyone who values science. In early 2015, months before the damning Wall Street Journal report, Stanford University professor John P.A. Ioannidis penned a critique of Theranos’ lack of peer-reviewed research in JAMA. Theranos responded by siccing its lawyers on Ioannidis in an attempt to get him to retract his opinion. That’s sketchy as hell — especially for any biotech or health tech company.

Based on these criteria, Theranos and Haemanthus set off a cacophony of obvious warning bells. But they’re not the only ones. Every year at CES, there are plenty of health tech startups peddling dubious concepts and vaporware right next to people genuinely doing the work. Health is the most valuable thing anyone has, so it’s not always easy to see false promises when your eyes are clouded by hope. No one wants to be sick, and technological miracles are an easier pill to swallow than the protracted ups and downs of real science. But if there’s one thing I took away from You Can See Everything, it’s that Theranos’ playbook is still, unfortunately, alive and well.

items.title: Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
paragraphs: Chancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a £4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defence Investment Plan.
The reductions come on top of the 1% cuts departments were asked to make earlier this year in order to pay for the initial £10.3bn of the plan's overall £15bn price tag.
The plan boosted defence spending; however the chancellor continues to come under pressure to explain how he will meet a further target of spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the chancellor of only offering "a plan to have a plan" adding: "I bet [Vladimir] Putin's really scared now."
Setting out his Budget, Healey hinted that meeting that goal would require further cuts, telling MPs it would involve "looking hard at public spending".
He said he would set out how the UK would reach the 3% target by 2030, as well as 3.5% of GDP by 2035, at next year's spending review.
Government departments have yet to decide what will be cut from their capital budgets.

Capital budgets are focused on long-term investments, rather than day-to-day spending. For example, earlier this year, when departments had to make capital budget cuts to fund the initial defence spending rise, a number of major road improvement schemes were scrapped.
Badenoch criticised Healey for not using his Budget to explain how he would boost defence funding to 3%.
"He is the man who is making our country less safe. He has failed his own test. This is on him, and no one will ever forget," she said.
The Conservatives have previously urged the government to pay for defence by making cuts to the welfare budget.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the UK was on "a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato Allies in The Hague - to ensure we're all investing what's needed to remain ready & able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security".
Chair of the Commons defence committee - and Labour MP - Tan Dhesi said "some of the key decisions on defence spending have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review".
He added: "There is a cost to inaction. Investment in our nation's defence and security cannot be kicked into the long grass."
Earlier this year, Healey resigned as defence secretary, accusing the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer of not providing enough money to keep the UK safe.
In a scathing resignation letter, he specifically emphasised his belief in the importance of reaching a 3% target by 2030.

Now chancellor, Healey told the House of Commons on Wednesday: "At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030.
"And today, I am getting work under way to get there in a fiscally sustainable way."
In addition to looking at public spending, Healey said he also wanted to use "more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies".
starting treaty negotiations with Finland, Poland and Netherlands to set up a "multilateral defence mechanism" which would allow allies to share resources
increasing the amount of private investment in defence through public-private partnerships
directing the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to put £5bn into "defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability"
The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the UK government's target to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 will cost £35bn.

Helen Millier, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Increasing investment in defence companies may contribute to the target but it is unclear how much this will lead to an increase in UK defence capabilities.
"There is much further to go to get to 3% of GDP on defence and it is hard to believe that this government will want to get there without topping up spending totals."
In his Budget speech, Healey also announced £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine, in the form of loans and export guarantees.
The funding includes £5.5bn of loans through World Bank guarantees and a grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association's crisis facility.
A further £3bn will be made available to Ukraine through loans facilitated by UK Export Finance, a government export credit agency.
Healey told the House of Commons that the week had started with Russia launching a "brutal ballistic missile attack" and that the extra money would send "a clear message to Moscow".
He said that when he told the Ukrainian leader about the additional support in a phone call, President Volodymyr Zelensky had said: "You've made my day."
Later on social media, Zelensky welcomed the money, saying: "Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realising that it must end this war of its own making."
The money comes on top of the UK's pledge to provide Ukraine with £3bn of military support until at least 2030-31.

items.title: Renowned Iranian Filmmaker Sentenced to Prison, Asset Confiscation
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

The Tehran Revolutionary Court has sentenced Jafar Panahi, the renowned Iranian director and filmmaker, to five years and one month in prison. The court also ordered the total confiscation of all his property, a two-year ban on social media activity, and a two-year travel ban.

Panahi’s defense attorney, Mostafa Nili disclosed the verdict to the news website Emtedad, revealing the sentence was issued in absentia and "without scheduling a court hearing" by Branch 26 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court.

Explaining how they learned of the sentence, Nili added: "Last week, we noticed that Mr. Panahi’s bank accounts had been frozen. Upon visiting the sentence execution branch of the Culture and Media Prosecutor’s Office, we learned of his new sentence."

Jafar Panahi, director of It Was Just An Accident and winner of the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival, returned to Iran via land border crossing in late March 2026, following the Oscar campaign for his film.

Panahi’s return to Iran came after he had previously been sentenced in absentia to one year in prison, a two-year travel ban, and a two-year prohibition from joining political or social organizations on charges of "propaganda against the state" - citing allegations of "making subversive underground films against the government," supporting political prisoners and protests, and backing the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement.

The U.S. Department of State has previously cited the restrictions imposed on Jafar Panahi in its human rights reports on Iran, highlighting his travel ban and prosecution on charges of "propaganda against the Islamic Republic" as prominent examples of the suppression of freedom of expression and artistic activity in the country.

The State Department also noted that the Islamic Republic imposes widespread restrictions on cultural and artistic freedoms through strict oversight of film production and screening, censorship of cinematic works, and the prosecution of critical filmmakers.

Additionally, the U.S. Department of the Treasury previously sanctioned two Revolutionary Court judges, Abolghasem Salavati and Mohammad Moghiseh, for their roles in penalizing citizens for exercising their rights to freedom of expression and assembly.

When announcing those sanctions in December 2019, the Treasury Department emphasized that Iranian artists, including filmmakers and poets, have been prosecuted on charges such as "propaganda against the state" and "assembly and collusion against national security" solely due to the content of their creative work.

Acclaimed Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi is one of the few directors in cinema history to win top honors at the world’s major European film festivals, having earned the Golden Lion at Venice, the Golden Bear at Berlin, the Golden Leopard at Locarno, and both Palme d’Or and the Caméra d'Or at Cannes

items.title: Here’s how macOS is changing for touchscreens
paragraphs: Touchscreen laptops are nothing new in the Windows world, but Apple has only just announced its first MacBook with a touchscreen. Apple isn’t rushing to change a bunch of things in macOS to optimize for touch, though: Most of the touch action will be in the apps themselves, it seems.

As far as major macOS changes go, iOS’s Dynamic Island will debut on the new MacBook Pro, and Apple touts the added touch controls as particularly useful for interacting with the interface to accept AirDrops and pause music playback.

Otherwise, Apple gives some pretty predictable ways that the touch input will work with the new MacBook Pro. You’ll be able to pinch and zoom in on photos, drag and drop slides between two different presentations, and swipe to scroll through webpages. Which, yeah. That’s how touchscreens work.

The more interesting stuff will probably happen in individual apps. Unsurprisingly, Apple’s apps will already be “optimized” for touch, and the system will automatically translate touches into clicks. Apart from that, Apple lists a handful of third-party apps that will take advantage of the new touch controls, including Notion, Canva, Zoom, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Lightroom, and DaVinci Resolve. Adding the possibility of multitouch to some of these pro creator apps is interesting, but for the most part, it seems that touch will merely be a secondary input mechanism rather than a whole new way of interacting with the entire system. You’ll be able to double tap to make a window full screen the way you can with a double click, and you can drag the corner of a window to resize it.

All told, this is shaping up to be a year of interesting hardware moves from Apple. The company just launched its first folding phone in the form of the iPhone Duo, with preorders backed up into 2027. Earlier this fall the company also launched the HomeView, its first display for the smart home. And it’s been an equally spicy software story for Apple this year, too. The Apple Watch is about to take its first steps into the land of wearable surveillance, Siri is actually kinda good again, and MacOS scored an easy win just by dialing down the Liquid Glass effect. Why not throw in a touchscreen MacBook and a touch-optimized MacOS at this point? The Ternus era is off to a running start.

items.title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
paragraphs: If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into the bank account that you use to pay it, from the start of January.
Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.
However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.
Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way of giving them the payments.
This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.
The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.

items.title: Government minister calls for review of 'unacceptable' BBC Scotland channel closure
paragraphs: The BBC said a wide range of its programming currently shown on the linear TV channel would be available online or on BBC One or BBC Two in Scotland.
Shows include Scotland's Home of the Year, Murder Case, Inside Barlinnie, the Scottish Cup Final and Hogmanay.
The current plans won't see any changes to BBC Scotland's main news programme Reporting Scotland, which is shown on BBC One or the broadcasters radio or online services.
After the announcement, Director of BBC Scotland, Hayley Valentine said more cuts could be on the way.
The BBC previously announced it would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 - almost one in 10 jobs - as part of measures to make £500m savings in the next two years.
In June, 550 job cuts were announced in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage of cuts.
In recent months, the BBC announced a series of closures of programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus.
Cuts to radio programmes have also been announced.
The broadcaster, which has about 21,500 full time employees, gets most of its income from the licence fee, but the number of TV licences sold has been declining in recent years.
An Ofcom spokesperson said: "While decisions about closing a service are a matter for the BBC Board, Ofcom's role is to hold the BBC to account for delivering its mission and public purposes.
"We will be engaging with the BBC to understand how it plans to serve audiences across the UK in light of its proposed changes and will respond to the cabinet secretary in due course."

As a public service broadcaster, the BBC's mission is "to act in the public interest, serving all audiences through the provision of impartial, high-quality and distinctive output and services which inform, educate and entertain".
The proposed closure of the BBC Scotland TV channel as a linear service is proving highly controversial.
Many within the TV industry saw the move as almost inevitable. Audiences for traditional broadcast television are falling and BBC funding is under huge pressure.
There was the question of whether the linear channel was sufficient value for money. Would a focus on the iPlayer and opt-outs on BBC One and BBC Two better meet the needs of audiences?
Some programmes shown on the BBC Scotland channel get more viewers when they are repeated later on BBC One Scotland.
The Scottish government's opposition to the proposal runs deep.
But it has no power to stop the move. Broadcasting is a Westminster matter.
TV regulator Ofcom helps to ensure that the BBC serves its public service purposes and serves all audiences.
But it does not have the power to simply compel the BBC to provide a particular linear broadcast service.
Its interest in this issue is likely to be more holistic.
It may, for instance, examine whether the BBC is serving Scottish audiences adequately and how the linear TV channel's closure would affect this.

items.title: Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered
paragraphs: John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.
It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.
While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.
The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament, a sign of how much the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.
Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%
However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.
The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.
As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.
The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.
So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.
There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.
And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.
Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.
Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.
And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.
Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.
So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.
With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.
The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.
So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.
For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.
A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

items.title: Apple ‘Pro and Tell’ event: Everything announced this week
paragraphs: Apple closed out its week of product announcements with its “Pro and tell” event on Wednesday, where it took the wraps off its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro. Though Apple may have saved its biggest and most exciting update for last, it revealed a few other device upgrades and updates in the days leading up to its big reveal. We’ve rounded them all up here.

Apple CEO John Ternus revealed the company’s first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen, allowing you to perform gestures on your screen like scrolling, swiping, and pinching. The company says the touch sensor is “built directly into the display panel,” not on top of it, which helps to reduce latency.

The device also offers a tandem OLED display, a 120Hz refresh rate, and 2,000 nits of brightness. It’s also lighter than previous MacBook Pro models, with the 14-inch model weighing three pounds. The device brings back the illuminated Apple logo on its lid as well, and is the first to come with a Dynamic Island for viewing real-time updates, searching for files, and using Siri AI.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display starts at $2,899 with a 14-inch display and M5 Pro chip, while the 16-inch version starts at $3,399 with an M5 Pro. There are also configurations available with an M5 Max chip. The touchscreen MacBook is available to preorder starting today, with availability starting November 6th.

Apple has upgraded its iPad Mini with a larger, 8.5-inch OLED display. The device is just 5.4mm thick, with bezels that are 24 percent slimmer than the previous generation. It also comes with a new “Acoustic Display”, which Apple says includes woofers paired through the display for better bass and more volume.

Along with these updates, the iPad Mini also comes with Apple’s more powerful A20 Pro chip, a 12-megapixel camera in landscape orientation, and an IP67 rating for protection against water and dust. The iPad Mini starts at $699 for Wi-Fi only and 128GB of storage, and comes in “midnight” and “starlight” colors. There’s also an option for a glare-reducing nano-texture display with the pricier 256GB and 512GB configurations.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro now comes with Apple’s new M6 chip, along with the company’s in-house N1 networking chip that adds support for Wi-FI 7 and Bluetooth 6. The device also has three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports with support for charging and DisplayPort connectivity, ports for MagSafe 3 and HDMI, as well as an SDXC memory card slot.

Similar to its predecessor, the M6 MacBook Pro also offers a Liquid Retina XDR display with a nano-texture option, as well as a 12MP Center Stage camera. You can preorder the new MacBook Pro today, which starts at $1,999 with a 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, 16GB of memory, and 1TB of storage. Devices start shipping on November 6th.

Apple’s latest lineup of iMacs comes with the company’s new M6 chip as well, which the company says “delivers up to 5x faster on-device AI performance” than the previous M4-powered iMac. It also sports Apple’s new N1 wireless networking chip.

Not much else has changed with the M6 iMac, as it offers the same design and color variations as its predecessor. It also still comes with up to four Thunderbolt ports. The M6 iMac starts at $1,499 with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, 16GB of memory, 256GB of storage, and two Thunderbolt 4 ports. Preorders open today, with availability starting November 6th.

Apple is updating Keynote, Numbers, and Pages with an AI chatbot that the company says can understand the context of the document you’re working on. The chatbot is built using models from Apple and OpenAI, allowing it to do things like design and animate slides in Keynote; create and restructure drafts in Pages; and calculate and visualize data in Numbers.
The company is also bringing an AI-powered fill feature to Pixelmator Pro, a new AI assistant in Logic Pro, and direct access to MotionVFX in Final Cut Pro.

items.title: Watch Apple’s reveal video for the touchscreen MacBook Pro
paragraphs: is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Apple just announced its first touchscreen MacBook at its “Pro and tell” event on Wednesday. It showed off the long-awaited touchscreen in a video of the new MacBook Pro during the event that you can watch right here to see the new display in action.

The new MacBook Pro’s PROLED XDR touch display is a tandem OLED panel with up to 2,000 nits of brightness and a 120Hz refresh rate. It features a hole punch for the webcam, rather than a notch. Apple says the new laptop weighs as little as 3 pounds. It also brings back the glowing Apple logo on its lid, which Apple CEO John Ternus teased in a video on X.
Preorders for the touchscreen MacBook Pro open today, and it will be available on November 6th, starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch model or $3,399 for the 16-inch.

The touchscreen MacBook has been a long time coming, even by Apple’s “fashionably late” standards — touchscreens have been mainstream on Windows laptops for well over a decade now. It was rumored for years before finally becoming a reality, much like the new iPhone Duo. Both devices are among the first Apple launched under its new CEO, John Ternus, who formerly led hardware engineering at Apple.
Earlier this week, Apple also announced a new entry-level MacBook Pro, M6 iMac, and an OLED iPad Mini.

items.title: Hands-on with Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro
paragraphs: Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one. Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface. While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly.

The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models. The difference is even bigger when you jump to the 16-inch model, which clocks in at 4 pounds, while the M5 Pro version without a touchscreen is 4.7. When picking up the 16-inch, you immediately notice the newfound lightness. It still has heft, but it feels better balanced when picking it up from a corner with one hand. Putting it side-by-side with a current 16-inch MacBook Pro, you see that it’s slightly thinner and has a footprint a smidge smaller. Aside from that, the feel of the materials is just like the MacBook Pros we’ve had for several years now.

Also exciting is the return of the glowing Apple logo. It’s a seemingly minor feature, but one that definitely got the audience excited during the introduction, and marks the return of a bit of flair to the MacBook lineup which, let’s be fair, has grown a bit utilitarian-looking over the years. Like the illuminated lid logo from years back, its brightness matches your screen, so it dims and can be fully turned off.

Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps. You can swipe directly on the screen to scroll through websites, pinch to zoom, and double-tap to maximize a window. Some third-party apps might need to be updated to take advantage, but they shouldn’t be completely useless since macOS simply translates taps to clicks as a fallback. That said, anyone who has tried to “click” a tiny button in an app with their finger knows it’s a pretty fiddly experience at best, and infuriating at worst.

Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top-left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app. Similarly, tapping to open a drop-down menu magnifies it, giving you a bigger target. And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps towards the top of the screen.

The Dynamic Island is a nice improvement over the notch, though. It’s so small and tucks nicely out of the way. Things like your music currently playing will live up there, and you can tap it for quick controls. When you change the brightness or volume, that’s also where you’ll see the slider pop out from, rather than the upper right-hand corner.

The screen itself is gorgeous. No surprises there. The OLED is punchy, bright, contrasty, and saturated. All the adjectives you want to hear about a display. But it’s not like the Liquid Retina display was some sort of slouch. Without more time to do side-by-side comparisons, it’s hard to tell just how much of an improvement the OLED XDR display is.

On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook. And not having Pencil support just seems like a huge missed opportunity. That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant, and not an entirely new product line. Unsurprisingly, there is a price premium for the new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. The touchscreen OLED model starts at $2,899, $400 more than the otherwise similarly-specced M5 Pro MacBook Pro.
