items.title: US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta dies aged 96
paragraphs: US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta has died at the age of 96, her family has announced.
Huerta campaigned alongside fellow labour leader Cesar Chavez for farm workers' rights in the 1960s and 1970s, founding the United Farm Workers Union (UFW) with him.
Through her foundation, Huerta had continued her activism work addressing immigration and voting issues.
"As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family," family spokesman Erik Olvera said on Wednesday.
Born in New Mexico, Huerta grew up in Stockton, California, in the heart of the state's large agricultural industry. She was raised by her mother, who at one point worked at a cannery.

Huerta first became a teacher after graduating from university, before turning to organising workers. She later worked on civil and women's rights, as well as environmental issues, all while raising 11 children.

"I would like to be remembered as a woman who cares for fellow humans," she is reported by multiple sources to have once said. "We must use our lives to make the world a better place to live, not just to acquire things. That is what we are put on the earth for."
Earlier this year, Huerta said Chavez, who died in 1993, had "manipulated and pressured" her into having sex and on another occasion forced her in the 1960s.
That was after the New York Times published an investigation detailing allegations from Huerta and two other women, who said Chavez groomed and sexually abused girls involved in the labour movement.
Huerta said the two encounters with Chavez resulted in pregnancies that she chose to keep secret, arranging for the children to be raised by other families.
Chavez's family said in a statement at the time that they were "devastated" by the reports and praised the women's "courage to come forward".

The UFW was among those paying tribute to Huerta, who reportedly died of cancer, on Wednesday, saying in a statement posted to social media that she had coined its motto - "Si Se Puede!", Spanish for "Yes, we can!" - which became a familiar rallying cry for activists seeking better working conditions for Hispanic farm workers.

"Her life's work was to empower her community to face and overcome injustices, and she has left farm workers and the entire Latino community stronger and more organised than she found it," the UFW said.
"Her commitment to civic engagement and bringing political power to disenfranchised people is a lesson we all should carry to the ballot box."

Huerta also helped end what was known as the Bracero Program, where Mexican men were brought to work temporarily into the US, and helped negotiate the 1986 Immigration Reform Act, according to the union.

The president of the voting group Voto Latino, María Teresa Kumar, called Huerta a "civil rights giant" who gave "her entire life, until her final days, to championing and fighting injustice for everyone, no matter who they were or where they came from".
The Congressional Hispanic Caucus, made up of Democrats from the Senate and House of Representatives, said in a statement on Wednesday that "Dolores Huerta defied definition".
"A national and international icon, her legacy is woven into the fabric of our history," they also said. "Her fight for justice will continue to inspire generations. Rest in power, hermana."

items.title: Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster in Spain
paragraphs: Spanish journalist Roberto Gómez was dozing on the high-speed Renfe train, when it stopped and an announcement was made to passengers that there was congestion on the tracks.
The train eventually began to move again, he explained, and then the crash happened.
"The impact was terrible," he told Onda Cero radio. "You can imagine, the carriage is completely destroyed. All the suitcases are all over the wrecked carriage."
Gómez suffered only minor injuries but described another passenger falling on top of him and sustaining a deep gash on his head.
"We were able to help people who had suffered severe blows to their chest and ribs," he said.
Rafael Barcelo was in one of the worst-affected carriages. A bruise on his forehead makes him one of the lucky survivors. He was having a coffee at the time of the crash and "felt a huge impact".
"We were all thrown into the air," he told Reuters news agency at the site of the crash.
"I am reasonably OK, my friend is quite worse."
"I was travelling in coach seven, which is the one with more victims and the one most destroyed. I at least counted eight victims in that coach," he said, visibly shocked.
In the last carriage of the Renfe train, Miguel Ángel Pérez saw a similar scene.
"It was a terrible crash. The carriage partially overturned," he told Spanish TV program La Hora de La 1. "Luckily there were few people standing," he said.
The Spanish transport minister said the circumstances were "inexplicable".

According to regulations, under such circumstances, a train driver would be required to proceed at what is known as "sight speed" - about 40km/h (25mph), a speed that allows them to stop in time if they encounter an obstacle.

Officials will investigate what order the Renfe train got, if it was travelling at the usual speed for that section of track - "around 200km/h" according to the minister, and, more significantly, why did the operator not stop its journey when his screen would have displayed that another train on the same line was stationary.
"It isn't possible that our train was stopped for five or 10 minutes and that the other train wasn't told to stop," one of them said.

"How can this happen with the technology we have?," he added. "It's not normal. We weren't told anything. The person who should have been told something was the driver of the other train. We wouldn't have cared as long as the other train had been warned. I don't understand this."

items.title: Here’s where you can preorder the new OLED-equipped iPad Mini
paragraphs: Apple’s smallest tablet is getting a bigger screen. Earlier this week, the company announced the eighth-generation iPad Mini alongside several new MacBook Pro models, bringing OLED technology to Apple’s miniature tablet for the first time. The diminutive slate won’t hit shelves until November 6th; however, you can already preorder it from Amazon, Walmart, Apple, and other retailers in multiple colors starting at $699.

The forthcoming iPad Mini features an 8.5-inch OLED display, the largest screen the Mini has ever had, despite being both thinner and lighter than its 2024 predecessor. It also runs on Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which should deliver faster performance while supporting some of Apple’s new Siri AI features, including the ability to customize Siri’s voice. Apple has also introduced what it calls an “Acoustic Display,” which pairs speakers with the screen and frame to deliver louder, richer sound with deeper bass and clearer highs.

Other upgrades include IP67 water resistance and a 12-megapixel front-facing camera, now located on the long edge, making video calls easier in landscape mode. The new Mini also features Apple’s N1 wireless networking chip, which adds support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. Cellular models additionally get Apple’s new C2 modem, which promises up to 50 percent faster cellular speeds than the previous generation.

We haven’t had an opportunity to test the new iPad Mini (yet), but we’ll share our impressions once we get our hands on the new tablet at Apple’s “Pro and Tell” event. In the meantime, here’s everything you need to know.

As of today, you can preorder the new iPad Mini with Wi-Fi and 128GB of storage from Amazon, Walmart, Target, B&H Photo, and Apple in either black or a creamy white shade starting at $699. Best Buy is also currently accepting preorders and throwing in a $50 e-gift card with each purchase. Upgrading to the 256GB model at any of the aforementioned retailers will cost an additional $100, while the 512GB version will run you $999; the latter also features a more powerful six-core CPU, rather than the five-core CPU in the lower-storage models.

If you want cellular connectivity, the 128GB model is available for preorder starting at $849 at Amazon, B&H Photo, and Apple, while the 256GB and 512GB versions cost $949 and $1,149, respectively. Apple also offers a glare-reducing nano-texture display option on the 256GB and 512GB models, starting at $899 and $1,099, respectively. Opting for an LTE configuration brings those prices up to $1,049 and $1,249.
Update, October 28th: Updated to include additional retailers, specifically Amazon, Walmart, and B&H Photo.

items.title: Instagram doesn’t have a plan to pay long-form video creators
paragraphs: Instagram is testing long-form videos (again) to lure in creatives from YouTube, but the platform hasn’t figured out how (or if) it’ll actually pay them. After Instagram head Adam Mosseri announced Features on Monday, creators immediately started voicing their complaints on Threads and Reddit about the lack of monetization opportunities, compared to the ad share and performance-based incentives provided by YouTube.

Mosseri addressed the monetization concerns in a Threads post yesterday, saying “We understand the economics matter a ton, and are exploring multiple options to help long-form creators get paid.” It’s anyone’s guess what those solutions will look like.

In one post on Threads, creator Sidneyraz (real name Sidney Raskind) said it feels like Mosseri and Meta are “just making fun of us” by not giving creators the ability to place long-form monetization ads into Features videos. “Y’all know how this works and you know how ad calls work and you know that long form creators need ad rev to survive but you’re ask[ing] them all to upload long form content for free just to live on your platform,” Raskind said. “That’s insane.”

The new Features format is currently being tested by a small group of creators in the US and Brazil. Features videos can be up to 90 minutes long (compared to the 20-minute max for Reels), and seemingly focus on landscape content instead of vertical, making them a good fit for Instagram’s TV apps as it tries to snare our attention across more screens. Meta does have some limited monetization tools for Reels, but these don’t pay creators directly per view like YouTube does.

“What’s funny about Instagram adding long-form video and reels that link to the long form is the complete lack of any sort of monetization,” tech creator M. Brandon Lee said on Threads. “Why should I post my long form there? What benefit does it bring me? I can’t even post links in my content to make affiliate income unless I PAY you to post a LIMITED number of links. I can’t get ad share revenue. You want more but don’t give more.”

While some longer-form video creators on Facebook previously reported good earnings via its old ad revenue-sharing payout model, Meta retired this in 2024 when it switched to a performance-based system. The primary incentive to post a Features video is the reach of Instagram, but the tradeoff is knowing that Meta will use it to train its AI models. Google considers YouTube videos free game for AI training too, of course, but at least creators get paid by the platform.

Speaking on a podcast with Samir Chaudry and Colin Rosenblum, Mosseri said introducing pre-roll or mid-roll ads is “going to be problematic from a user experience perspective,” and that it doesn’t make sense to scale up the small existing performance-based program because Meta spends more money on it than it makes back.

“There are three ways you can get paid at a high level: you can get paid by the platform directly, you can get paid by a fan, and you can get paid by a brand. Right now how it works on Instagram primarily is that you get paid by brands, some people get paid by fans,” Mosseri said. “Creators don’t produce a lot more when we pay, compared to what they already create.”

items.title: Clock ticks down for Canada lotto winner to claim massive prize
paragraphs: Time has almost run out for a lottery winner in Canada to claim C$40m (£21.4m) in prize money, according to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation.
The winning ticket will expire on Wednesday "unless the rightful ticket holder comes forward", OLG said.

The corporation said the Lotto Max jackpot ticket was purchased a year ago at a retailer in Grey County, Ontario. The county - which includes the Blue Mountains and Owen Sound - is a popular tourist destination, which means someone may have bought the ticket and forgot to check it after coming home.
OLG told CTV News that the "sad part" was that the ticket had not been checked on the OLG app or at the store. It expires at midnight.
"We've been waiting, almost a year. It's going to be a year in a little less than 24 hours," Tony Bitonti, the media relations coordinator for OLG, told CTV.
OLG said the winning numbers for the jackpot are 06, 14, 17, 19, 26, 43, 45, with Bonus Number 27.
The lottery group said players should check places like clothing pockets, handbags, backpacks, wallets and vehicle glove compartments to try to find the ticket.
If it expires, the lottery will keep the $40m prize for future games.
If the 28 October 2025 prize goes unclaimed, it would not be the first time.

On 28 June 2022, someone in Scarborough, Ontario, won a $70m Lotto Max draw, but no ticket holder ever came forward. OLG said at the time that 2,700 people called and emailed about the ticket - but not one of them was the winner.
Atlantic Lottery - another government-owned corporation that manages lotteries - told Canadian media that about one per cent of prizes go unclaimed, often much smaller sums.
Last week, an Alberta resident won Canada's largest-ever lottery jackpot for $90m. The winner has yet to be publicly identified.

items.title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
paragraphs: Israel's election result is messy - here's why

Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.

With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.
Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.
Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.
With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from soldiers and diplomats yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.

Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.
If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.
During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades.
"It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.
He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction.
"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.
Benjamin Netanyahu called for "a strong right-wing national government"

Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc.

"The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."
Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.
Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority".
"We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."

The leader of the left-wing Democrats party told its partners in Eisenkot's bloc on Wednesday that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," Yair Golan wrote on X.

The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - appear to be heading for record representation because of a strong turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

The chairman of the Joint List, which has talked of providing an electoral "safety net" for the Jewish opposition, said on Wednesday that it was "ready and prepared to pave the way to oust the Netanyahu government".
"Change runs through a Jewish-Arab partnership - a genuine and equal partnership. Nothing less, and nothing more," Yousef Jabareen wrote on X.
Gadi Eisenkot said the Israeli public had "spoken in favour of change"

United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".
Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hardline, religious-nationalist trajectory.

Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.

items.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
paragraphs: Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety.

Officials said at least 68 people were killed on Wednesday morning after a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were believed to be carrying 544 passengers.

Speaking to reporters, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, traced the collision back to a security system that had stopped working at about 8.30am local time. The computer malfunction brought an estimated six trains to a halt along a 63km stretch of track.

Soon after, the central command in Madrid instructed one of the trains involved in the crash to resume service at normal speeds, sending it colliding into a train that was still sitting stationary on the tracks, said Puente. “It was the control centre – via its operators – that made the decision to resume operations, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he added.
State-owned rail operator Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”.
The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

Media on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network.
The first crash sparked conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued.

Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” the union said earlier this month.

Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.”
It has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo.

The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country where travel by train accounts for about 57% of all transport.

While the causes of the January crash remain under investigation, a preliminary report suggested that it could have been the result of defects in the track or in a weld between two sections of track. The report noted, however, that several other possibilities were also being investigated.

Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain.
The government says it has increased spending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018.

Spain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU.
Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.

Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials.

Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU.

On Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister said measures would be taken to rebuild trust in the country’s high-speed rail system. “Because it is simply unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have,” said Sánchez.
The crash was Spain’s worst rail accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

items.title: Key points at a glance
paragraphs: Here’s what you need to know from John Healey’s first Budget, as the chancellor sets out the government’s tax and spending plans.

items.title: Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures
paragraphs: This was a Budget I would describe as a flotilla of small measures.

Westminster is poring over the 150 page Red Book, external in which the Budget is printed and also what is formally called the Economic and Fiscal Outlook published, external by the watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility, the OBR.
The Red Book sets out the measures the chancellor will implement and how much they will cost. There are 98 of them, considerably more than normal and more than in either of Rachel Reeves' budgets.
But nearly all of them are pretty small in terms of their impact on the Treasury's spreadsheets.

This gets to the heart of why those involved in compiling this Budget have been irritated by commentary in the build up to it suggesting there would be nothing to see in John Healey's address – but also why those suggesting that were arguably onto something as well.

Firstly, as expected, it was a much smaller Budget in overall tax and spending terms than plenty of recent ones have been. But there were plenty of measures here and there which the chancellor will hope enough people notice and value – and others that some will likely curse.
There are more taxes for savers and landlords, for instance, and too for banks.

When a government has promised, as Labour have, to not put up income tax, national insurance or VAT – the big revenue generators – they end up looking elsewhere if they conclude putting up tax is necessary.

That runs the political risk of choosing particular sectors who might respond rather noisily. Think of the plenty of farmers who were incensed by the changes to inheritance tax Rachel Reeves was keen on.
The central challenge for Healey, which he shares with his recent predecessors, is the public finances are in a mess and so are the personal finances of so, so many households.

And there is a recurring sense of déjà vu in the language of the OBR. "The UK's economic and fiscal position remains very challenging," it says, with a splash of understatement, adding that "there have been further adverse developments" this year with in the conflict in the Middle East.

As for what happens, next, well, frankly, who on earth knows. Or, as the OBR puts it: "The outlook for the economy and the public finances is uncertain, with significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability."

The Budget book argues that "the UK economy is showing signs of resilience" but it is also true that the national debt, tax burden, inflation and interest rates are high, going up or both – and there could yet be further economic shocks that make things worse.
What happens, for instance, in the Middle East, once the mid term elections are done in America and the result of the Israeli general election is clear?

In short, the chancellor felt constrained in his capacity to act and his capacity to make a noticeable positive difference is perhaps constrained even more so – because any intervention, even expensive ones, may merely make a grim situation a bit less bad, rather than things actually feeling better.
Mitigating the bad is arguably a noble political aim, but it costs money and potentially comes with little political upside.
Instead there is this fleet of smaller measures that the government will hope gives their MPs something to try to sell – while acknowledging that they are not world changing.

Luke Tryl, the UK Director of the More in Common think tank, says: "The softly populist tone of this budget is likely to land well with the public. The Chancellor targeted groups the public have little sympathy with - banks, landlords, gambling companies and vape shops - and turned it into cost-of-living support, rate relief for small businesses and ensuring the state pension isn't taxed."

He adds: "Crucially, the chancellor may have avoided the biggest potential trap of the Budget - being seen to offer energy support for those on benefits and incurring the ire of the squeezed middle, who think they work hard but are left to fend for themselves.
"Instead, by offering support to all of those on Council Tax bands A to D, he is able to reassure them that the government will support them too."
The reaction of the opposition parties, from a range of different political perspectives, amounts to a critique that this Budget was thin.

The government counters that it is one piece in the emerging jigsaw of detail from the new-ish prime minister and his chancellor – with a plan help young people into work and cut benefits before Christmas, alongside a big picture sense of what the UK's long term relationship with the European Union could look like and a 10 year vision from Andy Burnham.

In summary, this felt like a cautious Budget. One critical friend of the government suggested to me this would be a "Mr Sensible Budget" – their hope and expectation that it might be shorn of bells and whistles, but shorn of timebombs too. Let's see.

items.title: Tory Brexit was ‘harder’ than promised in EU referendum, says Andy Burnham
paragraphs: Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum.

In another series of announcements connected to his plan to seek closer links with the EU, Burnham told ministers at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the current deal was a bad one, before writing to frontbenchers setting out his hopes to address this.

Brexit was also the main subject of Burnham’s exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, with the prime minister saying the UK had been “paralysed” by the lack of a Conservative plan after the vote.
A Downing Street summary of the cabinet meeting put his comments about Brexit above even those concerning the budget, which the chancellor, John Healey, was to deliver soon afterwards.

“The prime minister opened by setting out how he would shortly write to cabinet on the UK’s relationship with the EU,” it said, adding: “He said the Brexit deal left by the last government had been bad for the UK and had led to a harder Brexit than had been promised at the referendum.”

The letter to ministers made similar points, and ended with a warning from Burnham that they should not express opinions about the future shape of relations with the EU before a review of longer-term options.

“It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period,” he said. “It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.”

It follows reports that some ministers, including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the idea of a revised deal potentially bringing back the free movement of people to and from the EU, something Burnham has talked up as a possibility.

The letter set out Burnham’s two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will stay within Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement – a process that will formally kick off when the prime minister attends a European summit next month.
Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail.

“I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain,” he said in the letter. “It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration. It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.

“We hope the summit will lead to some important, concrete steps. Beyond it, we will need to consider the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan. I will set out the next steps for this process around the summit.

“Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.”

Any fundamental changes in the relationship “would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament”, he wrote, adding: “This is government policy to which cabinet collective responsibility applies.”
Challenged by Badenoch at PMQs about his Brexit plans, Burnham reiterated his criticism of the current deal, saying the UK “was paralysed by the party opposite” in the wake of the referendum.
In response, Badenoch said that Burnham had been using freedoms allowed under Brexit, for example, the ability to remove VAT from energy bills: “What he should be saying is: ‘Thank you.’”

items.title: How the Budget affects you
paragraphs: Families facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.
The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by hundreds of pounds in January.
Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money.
If you are living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, you will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment" from January, funded by extra tax on banks.
It will be paid directly into your bank account.

Council tax bands are listed below - you can check which one you are in by looking at your annual bill or checking the government's website, external, although that was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement.
Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive the equivalent funding, and they will decide whether to introduce the same payment.

This is designed to help with soaring energy bills, with some forecasts suggesting a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January the saving will be only a portion of that. Although it's designated for energy bills, you can spend the money on anything you wish.
The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was introduced in October, will also be extended to July. It was due to end in April.
The fee for connecting to your gas supply so called standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales, next year "or as soon as possible after", the chancellor said.
These fixed daily charges will then be shifted onto the price you pay for each unit of energy.
The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will save an average of £45 a year, with lower users gaining the most. But the saving will come after the projected big rise in bills in January.
Higher users - in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families - will pay more than they currently do.
The government wants to extend reforms to electricity standing charges later.
The 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, will be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.
It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52.95p per litre.
Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.
The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.
The chancellor has scrapped his predecessor's plans to reduce the annual amount people can save tax-free in cash in Individual Savings Accounts (Isas).
Rachel Reeves had wanted the policy to encourage personal investment in stocks and shares.
It meant, from April 2027, if you're under 65, you would only be able to save £12,000 a year in cash in an Isa, rather than £20,000.
Instead, the government plans to create a new "Starter Isa" for first-time investors.
If you have a large amount in savings, or if you fail to use the tax-free Isa allowance, then you will pay more tax from April.

You do not pay tax on all savings. There is the annual £20,000 Isa allowance, and an annual savings income allowance (in other words, the interest received on a savings pot) of £1,000 for basic rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate taxpayers.
But beyond that savings tax rates will rise by four percentage points to 24% and 44% respectively from April.

Landlords could also pay more in tax. In analysis published on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said these steps along with measures over the past decade that have reduced private landlord returns "collectively risk leading to a steady rise in rents".
Minimum wage rates will rise by 3.9% in April. It means:
Eligible workers aged 21 and over on the National Living Wage will receive £13.21 an hour, up from £12.71
If you are aged 18, 19 or 20, the National Minimum Wage will increase to £11.27 an hour, up from £10.85
For those aged 16 or 17, the minimum wage will rise to £8.31 an hour, up from £8
The separate apprentice rate which applies to eligible people under 19 - or those over 19 in the first year of an apprenticeship – will also increase to £8.31 an hour, from £8
However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.
For all workers, the ongoing freeze in the income bands, or thresholds, at which income tax is paid went unmentioned in the Budget.
But it means any kind of pay rise could drag you into a higher tax bracket, or see a greater proportion of your income taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands.
The triple lock policy means that the state pension will go up in line with average wage increases, at 3.9%.
the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now
the old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now
The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.

The chancellor said this would be the case until at least 2030, as there will be a new Pension Tax Allowance, so pensioners with an income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax.
The First Time Buyer Isa has been in the planning stages with the government for a while.
Healey has confirmed that it is intended to replace the often-criticised Lifetime Isa.
The penalty for withdrawing savings from a Lifetime Isa if you are buying a home above the £450,000 threshold will be scrapped.

Separately, he confirmed the Your First Home equity scheme to allow first-time buyers in England to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.
The government has made no changes to student loan rates - saying only that it is being "kept under review".
There has been some backlash after the previous chancellor froze the repayment threshold for Plan 2 student loans, which were given out for just over a decade in England from 2012.

It means the salary at which borrowers start paying back their loans is due to stay at £29,385 in April and remain there for three years – so graduates start repaying sooner and repay more each month than they would otherwise have done.
Some announcements affecting your finances have already been made by the government.

Tariffs removed from 100 food items such as baked beans and garlic, which the government calculates could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June
Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030
Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period
Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that

The prime minister's plan to reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares in England from January to be in effect throughout 2027. Some cities already have caps, and funding is being given to the devolved nations

items.title: They did it! Sennheiser HD 480 Pro are the best closed-back headphones I’ve heard (and it's not even close)
paragraphs: The Sennheiser HD 480 Pro is the new benchmark in closed-back sound quality, offering a balanced, neutral sound profile with a touch of added bass warmth. It's rich and detailed mids are exceptional, and its smooth treble will be enjoyed by the maximum number of people. Critics will think it lacks the excitement of some audiophile headphones, but if you want correct-sounding headphones that will present your favourite music in the absolute best light, you can't do better than the Sennheiser HD 480 Pro.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
I first fell in love with audiophile headphones because they offered so much more clarity, technicalities, resolution, and other words that basically mean perceived detail.

Price: $399 / £339 (just headphone); $439 / £369 (with hard case)Release: April 2026Driver & housing: 38 mm dynamic driver; closed-backMaterial: Matte composite body, metal headband slider, washable velour/fabric acoustic ear padsCable: Detachable single-sided cable connecting via a 4-pin mini-XLR port (pluggable to either ear cup); 3.5 mm straight jack with screw-on 6.3 mm adapterImpedance: 130 Ω (at 1 kHz)Sensitivity: 107 dB SPL (1 kHz / 1 Vrms) / 98 dB SPL (1 kHz / 1 mW)Weight: 272 g

The pair that first opened my eyes was the Sennheiser HD 550, and they blew me away because their neutral/bright sound profile encouraged me to focus on higher frequency detail that I otherwise wouldn’t have noticed. The HD 550 also offers an excellent midrange with natural timbre, but it was the exciting treble that I fixated on.

The $400 Sennheiser HD 480 Pro isn’t here to excite you. Made for studio pros, specifically for tracking and mixing, the 480 Pro isn’t made for audiophiles, so instead of throwing fireworks at you, it paints a neutral, balanced, correct-sounding sound profile.
The result is the best closed-back pair of headphones that I’ve yet heard, and my new go-to recommendation if you’re looking for a set of the best-sounding headphones on sale today.

Overall, Bass and treble are gloriously well balanced without overshadowing the midrange. That’s a feat for any type of headphone – including the more forgiving open or Bluetooth sets – let alone a closed-back pair. The overall sound is correct-sounding with a touch of warmth. Nothing is out of place, and listening to music I’ve been familiar with for several decades, it all just sounds as it should.

The only negative aspects to the 480 Pro are preference-based, as opposed to glaring tuning errors. For example, you might prefer a different approach to treble than the 480 Pro – yet the 480 Pro’s treble is the best version of its approach that I’ve heard. All together, this is an exceptional-sounding headphone, and the best closed-back I’ve ever used.

Bass: This bass is full with plenty of detail and slam, putting a focus on sub bass yet still offering plenty of mid-bass punch. I find this presentation detailed, with some nice ‘grip’ to it. If I’m nit-picking, I can totally see it being too much bass for audiophiles searching perfect neutral, yet what’s on offer here doesn’t step on the toes of the midrange. It does, however, lend a warmth to things that some might not like (it’s definitely my jam).

You can get bigger bass in the far less expensive $160 FiiO FT1. However, you don’t hear bass in a vacuum, and where the FT1’s midrange’s clarity is hit by the wads of (wonderfully executed) low range, the 480 Pro’s overall balance remains faultless.

Playing Parliament’s Give Up The Funk, I love the fullness of the mid bass of Bootsy Collins in the intro. It has body and slam, backed up with a substantial sub bass that grounds the whole thing. On lesser sets that simply ramp up the bass, lower frequency details get lost easily, and listening to familiar music becomes frustrating – you can't hear the detail you know is there. That’s not the case with the 480 Pro. I get quality and quantity, and let there be no doubt, there’s plenty of quantity here!

Midrange: There’s more focus on the mid and upper mids, and less on the lower mids here. That makes the bass and lower mids seem more distinct, which is a presentation some people will love, and some will feel lacks cohesion. For me, the 480 Pro has the best of both worlds here, with the mid-bass being distinct enough from the mids so it hits hard, but not so much that the lower mids sound lean.

The ear gain region – the bane of many a headphone tuner – is exceptionally well done. I hear a little dip just before an elevation around 2.45kHz then again at 2.9-3.5kHz, followed by a noticeable dip around 4kHz. The former elevations are never too much, and serve as extra seasoning on male and female vocals.

4kHz is actually an area which usually gives me issues, so I tend to headphones that make a plateau around 2-4kHz instead of putting a spotlight on that area. The HD 480 Pro isn’t shy in this region, but it still doesn’t come across as shouty or grating. Instead, everything in the midrange comes across as timbrally correct. That’s basically the hardest thing to do with audio – any chump can make headphones sound ‘exciting’. The HD 480 Pro makes instruments and vocals sound correct, all balanced with each other. And when you put on a beautifully-produced track, the results are ‘right’.

For this review, I played through the Luxsin X8 DAC/Amp and the Mojo 2 by Chord. These pairings provided ample power delivery and headroom for the headphones, maintaining a transparent, uncoloured signal path from source to transducer. Music streamed via Spotify Lossless.

Treble: To my ears, there’s a generally relaxed approach to the lower treble that I initially read as dark. However, the more I listened to the 480 Pro the more I found Sennheiser’s approach to the treble was purposeful and in accordance with the balanced approach of the bass and mids.

I get a little spice around 6.6-7kHz, a dip around 8kHz, and then a little bit more around 9kHz. But as with the ear gain region, these slight peaks give added dimension to the sound, rather than sounding piercing or sibilant. In fact, this is the smoothest detailed treble I’ve heard, whether open- or closed-back. Michael Jackson’s remarkably bright Billie Jean has all its stabbing peaks rounded off, and Lucinda Williams’ jarringly sibilant Sweet Old World blends in rather than stands out. That never happens!

Of course, as I've said, a subtle, smooth, balanced treble isn’t everyone’s idea of audiophile-grade audio (Grado still sell headphones, after all). I happen to love the HiFiMan HE1000, with its comparably elevated treble profile. I love that it, along with its incredibly open ear cups, gives me a sense of crisp detail – it’s what I think of when I think ‘audiophile’. And yet, the HE1000 isn’t a practical set for everyday use. It’s a specialised headphone for specific moments. With its balanced sound, the Sennheiser is both an every-day set for YouTube doom scrolling and a specialised set for critical listening. It’s a rare bird in that it excels in every area, so that it may appear unexceptional. That's far from the case.

At $399/£339, the Sennheiser HD 480 Pro is in a competitive price bracket. It's also in a tricky spot for budget-conscious creatives who may look to the cheaper workhorse classic the Beyerdynamic DT 770 Pro ($200).

The value proposition here, however, is undeniable and convincing. Where the Pro DT 770 Pro offers bucket-loads of perceived detail with its incredibly elevated, sibilant treble, the 480 Pro offers unparalleled neutrality that can be enjoyed for hours on end without fatigue.

Closed-backs notoriously struggle with boomy bass, due to internal acoustic reflections and resonant standing waves trapped inside the sealed ear cup. But Sennheiser tames low-end clutter without muddying the mix. This is really very rare. Factor in the featherlight 272g build and washable components, and it’s a brilliant, durable investment. For me, at $400, this represents excellent value. After all, it's one of the best headphones I've heard, and it will last many, many years.
The HD 480 Pro slams just as much as the notorious Focal Azurys in the bass, but it's cleaner and clearer, without reverting to the overly-bright approach of the Focal set.
The Azurys is a very comfortable, cool-looking pair of headphones, but it offers more of a V-shape sound profile than the perfectly-balanced HD 480.

The upside of that is that the Azurys is a more exciting, dynamic pair of headphones. More bass and more treble mean more contrast. The midrange is really good with the Azurys as well. Yet it's not the star, as it's slightly overshadowed by all the excitement. You get none of these compromises with the HD 480 Pro.

For me, the smoothness of treble in the HD 480 allows everything to pull focus, whereas the comparatively sharper Azurys can sound almost hollow in comparison. And I think this is largely down to treble, as both cans sound very similar in the midrange (and certainly graph so).

The Focal Azurys retail for $599, though you can currently (and frequently) get them for more like $449 over at Amazon, and though I'd recommend them to certain people, I'd recommend the HD 480 Pro to everyone.

I have a soft spot for the FiiO FT1 – and not just because they are one of the best value pair of closed-back headphones in existence, at $165 over at Amazon. They sound fantastic, with their vaguely absurd levels of bass, which is plenty detailed and only messes with the lower mids a bit (coping much?!)

But A/B testing the FT1 with the HD 480 Pro, I still think it holds up... kind of. Sure it offers a more dynamic V-shape sound profile to the Sennheiser cans, but just like the Azurys, it does exciting well. The bass is definitely the boss here, but the midrange isn't just bullied around as is the case with so many bass cannons.

However, when comparing the treble responses, it's like comparing a scalpel to a sledgehammer. The HD 480 Pro walks a fine line between detail and sibilance. Going between the two with the glitchy, treble showcase that is K-Lone's slk, and where the FT1 ramps up the highs, shouting the detail to you, the 480 Pro seems to convey all the same high frequency detail, but with more body. I know that might sound weird, to refer to treble having body, but the 480 Pro just offers a fuller picture.
The Sennheiser HD 480 PRO is relatively easy to drive despite its 130 Ω impedance, because its sensitivity is reasonably high at 107 dB SPL (1 Vrms) or 98 dB SPL (1 mW).
What that means in practise is an M-chipped MacBook or modern PC will drive the HD 480 PRO effortlessly with ample headroom.

For music listening, a $9 Apple dongle will give you all the clean power you actually need. The only real limitation would be maximum volume if you're working with quiet, uncompressed studio recordings. Which I don't!
Bottom line: for the majority of music fans thinking about buying the HD 480 Pro, as long as you have a $9 Apple dongle, you're golden.
Build and comfort are big wins for the Sennheiser HD 480 Pro. Although it may look like a lot of other headphones, this set really is amongst the most comfortable out there.

It's the combination of light plastic, stainless spring steel, and soft velour ear cups that make this a durable, lightweight headphone that doesn't register even after hours of use. And with that steel, you know this headphone is going to retain its shape, no matter how it's treated.

This level of comfort is rare on a single headband headphone (ie, not headphones with dedicated comfort straps to distribute the weight on your head). I've previously had to add an additional Capra strap to make most single-band headphones bearable – such as the FiiO FT1, or the HEDD D1. And all these super light materials are replaceable – the detachable headband padding is even washable!

The width and depth of the ear cups is such that my average-sized ears never touch the driver housing, and the depth and soft materials of the cups means that the passive isolation is excellent. This is actually one of the highlights for me, as I work in a home office with my beautiful (noisy!) wife and a an equally beautifully noisy gaming PC. With the 480 Pro, I get to immerse myself in great sound, and not be distracted by either.

This is a well-designed headphone that's not built for show, but is built to last a very long time. For $400, this should be the standard – if I'm going to spend $400 on headphones, I want to be listening to them in 20 years time. And there's no reason that won't be the case with the HD 480 Pro.
I've given this pair of headphones a full five stars, so the answer is obviously, 'yes, yes, yes – of course you should buy it'. But that doesn't mean they're for everyone.

So, who is this headphone not for? I think any audiophile who wants a detail monster set that offers high-treble sizzle excitement and accompanying hearing loss, should give the 480 Pro a miss. Instead, pick up a HiFiMan instead (my current favourite is the HiFiMan HE1000 Stealth).

The Sennheiser 480 Pro doesn't get in the way of the music. It presents it honestly and clearly. It lacks the fireworks of the more exciting sets out there, but this is a pair of headphones that you can use all day every day with absolutely no issues – in sound or comfort.
If you want timbral accuracy, supreme comfort, and the passive isolation benefits of a closed-back, there is currently no better option than the Sennheiser 480 Pro.

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. items.title: Skulls, bulls and someone peeing in her own eye: four great exhibitions to see for free
paragraphs: Andy Warhol’s skull leers at Francisco de Zurbarán’s trussed-up little lamb from across the length of the gallery. Separated by hundreds of years – Warhol’s painting from the 1970s, Zurbarán’s from the 1630s – it’s an intergenerational conversation about still life’s staying power, and the inevitability of death.

This brilliant little show brings together still life paintings from way back in the past right up to the present day. There’s a gorgeous 1610-19 Dutch flower painting by Osaias Beert the Elder, and a vast vision of meats and cheeses with a pair of animal lungs hung grossly on a hook behind by Giovanni Battista Recco from the 1650s. There are piles of 19th-century French apples, vases of undulating 18th-century flowers. And then that little Zurbarán lamb – one of six he painted – glassy-eyed and morose, so laden with religious symbolism.

When we hit the modern era, there’s a lovely Pierre Bonnard painting of grapes and apples in sickly yellow and orange, a genuinely amazing Nicolas de Staël composition of stark, blocky bottles, lumps of pink rock by Philip Guston that look like cheese. Ignore the crap Picasso and the lumpen Juan Gris, and you get to come face to face with Warhol’s grim, grinning neon orange skull.

The whole show reinforces the idea that still life painting is terribly named. Because it’s not about life at all, it’s about death. Every fruit and vegetable in these works is about to rot, every flower is wilting, every animal carcass is about to go fetid. These are paintings of life’s fragility and precariousness. This is about how time is fleeting, how life is temporary. Mortality is written into every brush stroke.

Is this the greatest still life show ever put on? Does it have a tight curatorial concept? Does it tell an important story about the history and evolution of the genre? No, no and no. It’s just a bunch of really good, historic paintings. See, still life isn’t all just flowers and fruit. And even when it is, it’s pretty good.

Panting, his grey tongue hanging out, blood streaming down his back, the bull is on the verge of death. Paul Pfeiffer’s newest film captures the moment a matador plunges a sword into that bull’s back, but with no fanfare, no drama, no judgment. This is a film about ritual and spectacle, not about animal cruelty or cultural violence.

This isn’t Pfeiffer at his most attractive or impressive. Instead, this long, awkward, often ugly piece of art cinema zooms in on the faces of the crowd at a corrida, the hands of the saxophone players in the band, the colours of the walls, the patterns on the matadors’ clothing. It’s all the tiny details of this spectacle, the intricacies that make it tick.

It is, essentially, a film about how humanity creates spectacles to lose ourselves in, and how we repeat actions, sounds and movements to create some kind of meaning. The film is outwardly about bullfighting, but more widely about all rituals, religious or cultural. Is the corrida any different from going to church or a concert or a football match? In the end, we’re all just trying to find meaning by taking part, by belonging, by coming together and cheering as one. Throughout the film, people cheer, drink and eat, the band plays, a bull dies. That’s life, I guess. Joy and sorrow with some snacks in between.
Thomas Dane Gallery, London, until 19 December
Ebecho Muslimova has gone through the looking-glass, and what she has found on the other side is more worrying and uncomfortable than any kind of horror fantasy land. She’s found reality.

In every painting and installation here, Muslimova’s cartoon alter ego Fatebe is navigating a world turned upside down, spun on its head and inverted. Fatebe is a lewd, rude, nude comic book character, her naked body able to twist and contort, her face always plastered with a grin and her orifices always on display. One painting finds multiple Fatebes bent over, gleefully scrubbing parquet floors (a nod to a Gustave Caillebotte painting, this show is drowning in art history references) while another Fatebe makes a paper chain out of fabric she’s yoinking out of her nethers. Yet another work sees hundreds of Fatebes filing up the stairs of the gallery itself, but the plaster is crumbling and the print is peeling.

Fatebe is trapped under a glass like a spider, or she’s turned herself into the legs of a table. In one drawing she has grown two heads, one peeing into the other’s eye, the other defecating back in return.

All this gross-out weirdness and art historical density isn’t about fantasy and escape though. I think it’s about feeling pulled in endless directions, it’s about being stuck between the place you came from and the place you’re in now, it’s about discomfort and alienation. Or it’s about being able to wee in your own eye. Who knows, really. Either way, it works.

Back in 2013, a Palestinian fisherman found an ancient Greek statue of Apollo poking out of the sand. Thinking it was gold, they cut off a finger, but it was just beautiful, mottled green bronze. They tried to sell it on eBay, posting pictures of the sculpture laid carefully on Smurf bedsheets, but the authorities stepped in and confiscated the sculpture. No one knows where it is now, but Rosalind Nashashibi has painted it here, preserving its strange, almost magical history in hazy visions of green limbs on cartoon-covered sheets.

Not all the works are good, and the images of nudes and landscapes feel either like a distraction or filler. But the Apollo images are great. They’re like paintings of an autopsy, stark and unsettling. They’re filled with narratives – a clash of ancient art and modern cartoon, a beleaguered people finding hope of salvation in a gift from the gods, an act of care as those people gently try to preserve this sculpture on their softest bedsheets. Hope and despair, history and the present, all colliding in some often beautiful, washed-out painting.

items.title: Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader, feminist and civil rights icon, dies at 96
paragraphs: Dolores Huerta is seen at the California Democratic Party's 2025 State Convention at the Anaheim Convention Center in Anaheim, May 31, 2025. Court Mast/AP hide caption

Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase "Sí, se puede!" that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.

She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women's rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.

Huerta's resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation's most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to "Yes, it can be done" — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.
Dolores Huerta is seen at the California Democratic Party's 2025 State Convention at the Anaheim Convention Center in Anaheim, May 31, 2025. Damian Dovarganes/AP hide caption

Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.

This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement's co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died.
From the early 1970s on, Huerta's life partner was Richard Chavez, César's brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.
Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life's work and unravel all the progress made for workers.

When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: "It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I'll say it that way."

Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who went on to win a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.

Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.

Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students' poor living conditions.

"I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children."

Dolores Huerta looks at a mural of the late Cesar Chavez during a dedication of the Cesar Chavez Monument on the San Jose State University campus in San Jose, Calif., Sept. 4, 2008. Paul Sakuma/AP hide caption

Huerta's early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.

She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year "Delano Grape Strike." With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers.
Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.

She met U.S. Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and became a volunteer on his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her moments before he was shot.
The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing for farmworkers' rights.

Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating. In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush's opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco.

Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer's baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims.
After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus and hit the road to campaign for women's rights and encourage Latinas to run for office.
She also campaigned for Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden. California Gov. Gavin Newsom considered her a close friend.
Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores' 13 children, once pointed to his mom's courage during an interview, saying it was one of the most significant drivers of her life's work.
"To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farmworkers, to take on agriculture, which to this today is still a powerhouse. ... That took a lot of guts," he had said.

Huerta learned the art of lobbying politicians. She secured financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farmworkers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and fought federal guest worker programs.

By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass what would be the first state law recognizing farmworkers' right to collective bargaining.
Her work earned her many accolades. She was the first Latina to be inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame and she's received nine honorary doctorates from U.S. universities.
Schools are named in her honor in California, Texas and Colorado. Her image graces many murals, and streets bear her name, but she didn't always win favor with more liberal activists.

In 2016 when she endorsed Hillary Clinton instead of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont in the presidential Democratic primary, actor Rosario Dawson — a Sanders supporter who played Huerta in a 2014 movie about César Chavez — said Huerta had become "an instrument of the establishment."

Guitarist Carlos Santana later oversaw a documentary based on Huerta's life after the pair had a late-night conversation about music while in Hawaii. Santana, a Miles Davis fan, discovered Huerta was a huge fan of bebop legend Charlie Parker.
"I even met Charlie Parker. That's my claim to fame," Huerta joked during an interview with The Associated Press when she was 87.

It was her work as a leader within the labor movement that reverberated through the U.S. and beyond, making her name synonymous with civil rights. In the 2025 documentary "Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta," she recounted her decades-long journey in activism and talked about the inspiration she drew from the women's movement during the 1970s, saying it provided validation that she too could stand on the stage with other labor leaders.

"I hope that my legacy will be one of an organizer that organized to fight injustice," she said in the film. "We want to give our children an inheritance of justice, right, not jewels or property or money because they'll just fight over it. So the main thing to do is to give them this love for justice — and that is the greatest gift I think that any of us can have."

items.title: Tommy Robinson guilty of harassing two Daily Mail journalists
paragraphs: Political activist Tommy Robinson has been convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.
A jury at Southwark Crown Court found the 43-year-old, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.
The case concerned Robinson's response to Daily Mail and Mail Online articles from August 2024, showing him on holiday in Cyprus while riots took place in England following the Southport murders.
The court had heard how Robinson, from Bedfordshire, used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, forcing them to employ security or leave home.
Robinson had denied the charges, saying he had "panicked" and had been "scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".
He told the jury he felt the article had "endangered" his family by revealing they were staying in a hotel near Ayia Napa in Cyprus.

After the guilty verdicts, Frank Ferguson, the head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Robinson had "weaponised social media and subjected two journalists to a campaign of harassment which caused them serious fear of violence".​
Robinson was granted bail ahead of his sentencing, scheduled for 16 December‌.
Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, or up to 14 years if the offence is racially or religiously aggravated.

During the week-long trial, prosecutor Ben Holt had told the court that after three girls were murdered in Southport on 29 July 2024, Robinson had made a number of posts on social media. This had alerted the Daily Mail and Mail Online to the fact that he was in Cyprus.
The Daily Mail published articles with photos of the defendant, including one showing him "reclining on a sunbed using his mobile telephone".
Southwark Crown Court heard that over the following days, he responded with a series of posts on his X account.
On 4 August, these had included: "The daily mail have purposely gave the location of where I am with my children knowing full well that people want to kill me."
Robinson admitted hiring private investigators to take photographs of the home addresses of Dirnhuber and Young.
He said he had "wanted to find the journalists" to "put pressure on them".
But he told the jury he had not known they were "in fear."
"That wasn't my intention at all," he said.
"It was an attempt to bring the Daily Mail to the table."
The jury accepted the prosecution's case that Robinson had hired detectives to "intimidate" the journalists.
Photographs of Dirnhuber outside his home and cropped images of Young's family had been posted online by Robinson.

The court heard that, as well as social media posts and direct messages to Dirnhuber, the defendant had become "increasingly menacing" on a telephone call with Young on August 5, 2024, telling the freelance journalist: "I'm coming to get you."
Jurors rejected Robinson's claim that the Daily Mail had endangered his family by publishing the story.
He had wept in the witness box on Thursday as he spoke about his relationship with his children.
A police investigation had begun after the journalists reported concerns for their safety following posts on X that had contained their personal information.
A Met Police spokesperson said: "There are legitimate and established routes that can be pursued by people who have concerns or complaints about their treatment by the media."

They said, instead of following these routes, Robinson had issued "threatening online posts in the knowledge that they would almost certainly lead to his followers to target and intimidate those journalists".
The spokesperson said the journalists, fearing for their families' safety, had left their homes and hired private security.

The spokesperson added: "This kind of intimidatory behaviour is not acceptable, and anyone behaving in such a way to intimidate, harass and threaten others either online or in the real world can expect to be investigated and brought before the courts, as was the case here."
