items.title: Coca-Cola gives everyday heroes the royal treatment in posh portrait campaign
paragraphs: Coca-Cola has launched a wholesome new campaign honouring the local business people who support it. Local Royalty features four hand-painted portraits created by real royal portrait artists, proving that honour doesn't have to be dictated by blood.

While many ad campaigns are focusing on the digital side of design, it's a refreshing change to see Coca-Cola embracing analogue art. A campaign with heart and intention, Local Royalty demonstrates how stripping back to the tactile can create some of the best adverts.

The four portrait subjects were chosen to represent everyday people from hospitality and retail, including workers from a pub, corner shop, café, and fish and chip shop. Painted by artists who have previously captured royals such as Queen Elizabeth II, King Charles III, the Prince and Princess of Wales and Princess Anne, the stately portraits are a wonderfully unexpected homage to life's everyday heroes.

“Independent business owners create the places where local life happens, yet their contribution often goes unrecognised," says Rhona Stephen, senior director, communications for Coca-Cola Great Britain. "With Local Royalty, we wanted to celebrate them in a way that felt deliberately unexpected and enduring. By borrowing the visual language of official portraiture and placing these owners at its centre, the campaign gives their everyday impact the status it deserves.”

The portraits will be displayed as part of a free public exhibition at the Saatchi Gallery in London from 28th October to 1st November. For more creative news, check out Coca-Cola's new look or take a look at our guide on how to stand out as a portrait artist.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: You may get the right to find out what your colleagues earn - here's why
paragraphs: Employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning, the UK's equality watchdog has said.
Bosses should be required to respond to questionaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has proposed, external.
In addition, employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from carrying on, it said.
Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them.
At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about colleagues.

The EHRC urged lawmakers to make it compulsory for employers to provide information including colleagues' basic pay and hours worked, how employees' pay compares with each other, and information about bonuses, overtime, shift-premiums and performance-related pay, within a specific timeframe.
The rights watchdog argued that this would help cut pay discrimination, especially against women.
Women would also benefit from employers publishing salary details in job adverts, the EHRC has said previously, external.

items.title: Luminous viewpoint by Ryue Nishizawa rises within Japanese landfill site
paragraphs: A giant orange cone designed by Japanese architect Ryue Nishizawa acts as an observation deck at this large recycling complex on Shikoku island in Japan.

Nishizawa, co-founder of Japanese studio SANAA, positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin at Oono Associates, a recycling complex in the city of Toon, and open up this closed-off industrial space to the public.
Named Observatory, it was created for the inaugural edition of Setouchi Art and Industry 2026, an art and architecture festival held across industrial sites in Japan.

Specifically, it forms part of the Landscapes of Waste – A landscape shaped by nature, industry, and people exhibition, curated by Nishizawa’s studio partner Kazuyo Sejima, with whom he founded SANAA in 1995.
Nishizawa positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin within the vast recycling complex in Toon, Ehime, revealing the closed-off industrial setting to the public.
The bright orange cone measures 33 metres in diameter and four metres in height. Its size was intended to emulate an artificial hill.
Its luminous orange finish was chosen to deliberately contrast the blue-green hues of the surrounding landfill lining and landscape beyond it.
The platform encourages visitors to observe how the landscape is shaped by nature and human activity, and experience the processes of material circulation at the recycling plant.

Alongside Nishizawa’s observation platform, the Landscapes of Waste exhibition includes bus stops by architectural studio Shingo Masuda + Katsuhisa Otsubo, as well as buses and visitor workwear by Suzuko Yamada Architects.
Visitors are required to take these buses to the site and put on the workwear, as seen in the photos. The festival team said this brings “visitors themselves into the composition of the landscape”.
“Together, these interventions invite a closer encounter with the relationship between nature, industrial infrastructure and human activity,” it added.

Setouchi Art and Industry 2026 was organised by the Japan Industrial Art Foundation. Artists and architects were invited to work with industrial sites across Okayama and the Ehime prefecture on Shikoku to create a “decentralised museum” that opens these settings to the public.
Its inaugural edition runs until 31 October across seven venues, which also include a salt production site, a textile factory, a shipbuilder and a battery manufacturer.

“Developed through collaboration between artists and participating companies, the exhibitions offer access to industrial spaces usually closed to the public, revealing the technologies, materials and people behind everyday life,” said Setouchi Art and Industry.

“We hope that many people, including the younger generation, will re-examine Japan’s industries from a fresh perspective and discover the charm and potential hidden within them,” added Japan Industrial Art Foundation director Masahiro Ito.
Other recent projects by SANAA include the Taichung Green Museumbrary in Taiwan and a proposal for the National Museum of Ecuador.

items.title: At least 30 dead in crash between two trains in central Spain, media say
paragraphs: The scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press via AP hide caption

BARCELONA, Spain — A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 30 people on Wednesday in central Spain, according to local media.
Spanish authorities initially reported 10 deaths, but Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, added "that number will surely rise."
Spanish state-owned news agency EFE and other media reported later that the death toll had risen to at least 30.
It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain. One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García told TVE that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.

The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. It appeared the RENFE train rammed the IRYO train, Spanish media reported. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities."

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.
A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police to the crash site.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cancelled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo."
"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families."
The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, wrote on X that he was on his way to the crash site.

In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

items.title: A US woman feared dead was reported alive in Mexico. But cops now say that isn’t true
paragraphs: Arizona authorities say their Mexican counterparts were resoundingly mistaken when they publicly claimed recently that they found alive a woman who was feared slain after disappearing in 2024 – a turn of events that her sister has called “turmoil” and “heartbreaking”.
The case in question centers on Shayna Feinman, who was reported missing in rural Yavapai county, Arizona, in March 2024 at age 38.

Authorities believe she was walking to an acquaintance’s home when she was last seen – but she never arrived or returned to her dog, as the Arizona news outlet KSAZ reported. An ensuing search turned up Feinman’s car abandoned near where she had been staying with her boyfriend, Cavett Richards, according to the station.
Her wallet and identification reportedly were inside the vehicle, and her cellphone was ultimately recovered on nearby land.

Although Feinman had not been found, the Yavapai county sheriff’s office subsequently charged Richards as well as a man named William DalCerro with second-degree murder, conspiracy and concealing a corpse in connection with her disappearance. But the charges were dismissed, a $20,000 reward being offered for information as authorities kept investigating the case.

The secretariat for security and citizen protection in the Mexican municipality of Tijuana then delivered what initially appeared to be a startling update in Feinman’s case on Saturday, saying in a statement that she had been located in the city’s Encino neighborhood the previous day.

The statement from the secretariat had a picture of the woman sitting in front of a desk atop which was a missing poster with Feinman’s information. It asserted without elaborating that investigators had confirmed Feinman’s identity, noting that her physical characteristics matched those listed in her missing person report.

The woman had been put in protective custody while Tijuana authorities arranged for her to speak with the Feinman family and US consular officials, the statement said. The agency went so far as to post a link to its Saturday statement on a social media page belonging to Feinman’s sister, Kara.
But both Kara Feinman and the Yavapai’s sheriff’s office met the Tijuana officials’ statement with evident skepticism.
Kara told KSAZ in a story published on Monday that she was waiting for the Yavapai sheriff’s office “to know for certain” that Shayna had been found.

Though she acknowledged the woman in the picture released by Tijuana officials had “similar physical attributes” to Shayna, Kara struck a cautious tone, telling KSAZ: “I can only hope and pray [for] good news – but right now, we have to be realistic.”

Meanwhile, a sheriff’s office spokesperson told KSAZ that the agency was “aware of reports indicating that Shayna Feinman may have been located in Mexico” – but “at this time, the information remains unconfirmed”.

“There is insufficient evidence to verify her identity,” Yavapai sheriff’s office spokesperson Paul Wick added to KSAZ. Wick said the sheriff’s office was “actively investigating the matter” and would provide an update as soon as one could be “confirmed and … released”.

The Yavapai sheriff’s office published that update on Tuesday, when it said in a statement: “Today, US authorities confirmed to [office] detectives, utilizing physical evidence, that the individual located is not Shayna Feinman.”

The sheriff’s office alluded to prior media reports “regarding the alleged discovery of Shayna Feinman” that “were published without official law enforcement confirmation” – before saying its “detectives continue to work diligently with [her] family during this stressful time”.
Tijuana’s security and citizen protection secretariat did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In an interview with the Guardian on Tuesday, Kara Feinman said she believed the confusion about her sister possibly being in Tijuana initially stemmed from at least one concerned citizen who became convinced that she was there and made that known on social media.

She described being guarded about that possibility, reluctantly opening her mind in light of the Tijuana secretariat’s claims – and then enduring cyberbullying online by users who harshly judged her for not reacting effusively enough to the ultimately false news that Shayna had been found alive.

As she processed the reality that the search for the truth about her sister’s disappearance continued, Kara Feinman said her hope now was for those passionate about such investigations to realize how harmful it can be “jumping to conclusions without having all of the information” and then directing harsh words at the people most affected by those cases.
“Words are stronger than people think, and kindness can go so far,” Kara Feinman said. “It’s been turmoil going through this.
“It’s heartbreaking. It’s terrible, and I don’t wish this on anybody.”

items.title: XPPen Magic Pro 13 review: a premium Android drawing tablet for work and play
paragraphs: The Magic Pro 13 is a superb portable Android drawing tablet with an excellent pen and a simple connection to a PC, offering a premium experience whether mobile or at your desk.
Matt nano-etched glass with a paper-like feel, at 120Hz
Plugs into a PC as a drawing display over USB-C
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I liked the original XPPen Magic Drawing Pad because it showed that an Android tablet could be built around artists' needs. Its drawing surface felt closer to a desktop tablet than the glossy, slippery screens on most consumer devices, like an iPad or Samsung's Galaxy Tab series (read our guide to the best tablets with a stylus pen for drawing). I used it as a loose sketching tool, but accuracy issues kept me from replacing my desktop tablet, and I soon went back to my iPad Pro.

Three years on, and XPPen's new Magic Pro 13 fixes the biggest issues I had with the older first-time model. It has a processor that handles demanding art apps, a new stylus (importantly with 5,080 LPI resolution), a 3K 120Hz screen, and a USB-C connection that turns it into a PC drawing display. It’s also a good everyday Android tablet for video, email and Google Docs.

Wacom’s MovinkPad Pro 14 currently leads this category, and Huion’s Kamvas Pad 12 undercuts both, though its performance comes at the cost of a less impressive processor. The Magic Pro 13 sits closer to Wacom and Apple than the brand's old ‘budget tablet’ reputation, and it makes a strong case to be the one you pick, based on price, specs, and performance.

XPPen has come a long way from a disruptor to a genuinely impressive drawing tablet manufacturer; for example, its recent Artist Ultra 14 OLED tablet is an advanced desktop drawing tablet. The pitch with the Magic Pro 13 is that the same tech, minus OLED, can fit into an Android tablet.

Opening the box, I'm struck that XPPen hasn't overloaded the package with extras for the first time; you get the tablet, spare nibs, a drawing glove, and a high-quality USB-C cable for charging and PC connectivity. A case or stand would have been welcome, but that would have bumped the cost; besides, XPPen sells a stand, case, and magnetic keyboard separately, just like Apple.

A close look at the new tablet reveals a premium-feeling product. The white frame, curved edges, flat matte display, and discreet buttons make the Magic Pro 13's design choices closer to Wacom and Apple than the budget end of the market. At 655g and 6.65mm, it’s easy to hold for long stretches, which matters when you’re not propping it on a desk. I took it outside to sketch a local lane and also used it on the sofa, and it suits both.

The 12.95-inch screen gives you room to paint comfortably. For long, detailed desk sessions, some artists prefer a larger display; for example, you don't get the space to rest your wrist as you do with a desktop design, but as a tablet for all occasions, it's a nice size.

The Magic Pro 13 has two USB-C ports, but only one supports the high-bandwidth video connection needed for PC mode, so make sure you plug into the right one. Storage is expandable by microSD, which helps if you collect reference images and large art files. There are some quirks to the design; for example, XPPen has chosen to keep the rear camera that comes on standard tablets, a small lens in the top corner of the rear panel, which I thought could make drawing on the screen when laid flat a little awkward, expecting a slump or wobble, but it never happened.

The nano-etched glass has a matte, paper-like finish with a little resistance under the nib. The 3K panel covers 100% sRGB and 96% DCI-P3, with a peak brightness of 650 nits. At 120Hz, marks keep up with the pen, so it feels natural. The tablet display can toggle between 120Hz, 90Hz, and 60Hz, so you can balance battery life to how you use it; 60Hz, for example, is fine for browsing, and 120Hz is ideal for digital painting.

The X4 Smart Chip Stylus offers 16,384 pressure levels, a 2g initial activation force and 60 degrees of tilt. The 5,080 LPI figure is worth noting: it measures how finely the tablet resolves pen movement, separate from the number of pressure steps, and this is double the resolution of the original Magic Drawing Pad and on par with most high-end desktop drawing tablets.
The pen has enough weight to feel sturdy without tiring my hand; I draw for around two hours at a time and never get the kind of cramp that can creep in with slim styluses or cheaper, lighter pens.

To test tracking, I drew small circles, tapped dots, scribbled brush strokes, and repeatedly overdrew the same line. Lines stayed smooth, the cursor followed the nib, and I saw no jitter. That’s where the original Magic Drawing Pad fell short, and some recent budget tablets, like the Kamvas Pad 12, too. Side by side with Wacom’s Pro Pen 3, I couldn’t pick a difference.

My go-to Android drawing app is ArtRage (ArtRage 6 is on XPPen's free install list, but I use ArtRage Vitae); it's an older painting simulator with excellent traditional-media brushes and heavy paint tools that show quickly whether a tablet can keep up. I painted a quick sketch of a lane near my house, switching brushes and pushing paint around with the heavier tools. There was no visible lag, strokes landed where I aimed, and overall it's a really nice experience, close to using a desktop tablet.

The Dimensity 8300 processor, 8GB of RAM, and Android 16 handle painting and illustration well. Wacom’s MovinkPad Pro 14 offers 12GB, which gives it an edge with very large files. I tested the 3D sculpting app Nomad Sculpt on the tablet, and it was fine, with no issues; unlike the new budget Huion Kamvas Pad 12, the Magic Pro 13 didn’t get warm or have any issues, even in Performance mode. I’m not one for using massive amounts of layers; I rarely get past three and tend to collapse them regularly, but even when I did decide to add 10 layers and duplicate my painting to see what would happen, there was no slowdown or warming.

A key feature of the Magic Pro 13 is that it works as a standalone Android tablet and as a drawing display for a desktop or laptop. I plugged in the included USB-C cable, and it connected as a display, with the hardware handling the video link. I use an HP Omen Max 16 for gaming and art, and it worked seamlessly, with no need to download drivers or fiddle with the laptop or tablet settings.

Wacom’s MovinkPad Pro 14 offers a similar workflow, wired or over Wi-Fi, but it relies on a companion app on the PC to get it working. A wired connection also means turning on Developer mode and USB debugging on the tablet first. Those are one-off steps, and XPPen doesn’t offer a wireless option, but the XPPen route requires less setup and is literally a 'plug and go' solution.

I drew on the Magic Pro 13 away from my desk, then connected it to my computer to use my desktop art software, moving from ArtRage Vitae and into Rebelle. If you work at a desk all day, you’ll want a bigger screen, but for home work, travel, or hobbyists like myself who can’t justify both a tablet and a pen display, it covers both jobs really well.

The Magic Pro 13 ships with ibisPaint X and XPPen’s own Canvas app. I still prefer ArtRage for painting. Canvas adds Quick Draw, which wakes the tablet straight into sketching, and a doodle tool for annotating photos. It also keeps reference images from my shelf available alongside other work.

Split-screen and multi-app use work as you’d expect on Android 16, so I can check email or a web page mid-painting and return without losing my place. Performance mode suits artwork and demanding video, while Comfort mode cuts heat and suits browsing and Google Docs, though I didn't notice any heat during extended use.

The 13MP rear and 8MP front cameras cover video calls and reference snaps. I’ve been using the Magic Pro 13 on and off for three weeks, from general browsing to art creation; generally, the battery has lasted a couple of days before needing a charge.

The Wacom MovinkPad Pro 14 has a larger 14-inch OLED display with deeper blacks and 900 nits of peak brightness, plus a Snapdragon 8s Gen 3 chip and 12GB of RAM. It can also connect to a PC wirelessly (but, as mentioned, you need a companion app, since it's not a hardware solution). If screen quality, desk space, or a wireless link matters most to you, buy the Wacom.

By contrast, the new XPPen Magic Pro 13 costs around $100 / £100 less, has cameras the Wacom lacks, and connects to a PC through a hardware-level USB-C video link rather than a companion app for an easy solution. The recently released Huion Kamvas Pad 12 is cheaper, but the Magic Pro 13 sits a tier above it in screen, pen, and processing power – it's altogether closer to the experience of using MovinkPad Pro 14 or even an iPad Air.

The bottom line is that the new Magic Pro 13 is an accomplished, premium Android tablet with artists' needs at the centre of its design and workflow. If you want one tablet for drawing on the move and at a desk, this does the job: the stylus and screen feel natural, the original's tracking problems are gone, and it connects to a PC quickly. The Magic Pro 13 is the best option yet for artists looking beyond an iPad for an Android tablet, if you can live without the Wacom's OLED.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.
